speechtext:
ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT Mr. David Berger (Laurier) moved:
That this House condemn the Government for failing to provide adequate non-tax support for Reseach and Development and for its counter-productive policies and administration of tax support for Research and Development, including,
(1)	tax reform measures that disourage research and development by reducing funds available for R & D, by increasing the costs of R & D and by delaying investment in R & D facilities and delaying the introduction of new products and new processes, all of which generally impair the ability of Canadian companies to compete in global markets; and
(2)	management of R & D tax programs that has led to serious disagreements between industry and Revenue Canada over the kinds of activities that qualify for the investement tax credit for Research and Development resulting in long delays in obtaining refunds needed to finance ongoing Research and Development activities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this debate should be seen in the context of the commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to double national spending on research and development during his first term.
Mr. Speaker, I may recall that this commitment was made by the Prime Minister when he was Leader of the Official Opposition. Speaking to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce on March 22, 1984, four years ago, the Prime Minister said and I quote: "We intend to double our collective national commitment to research and development during our first term. This would make it possible to create hundred of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in new sales for Canada, on an annual basis".
However, since it came to power, the Conservative Government has reduced, not increased, support for research and development, the result being that our national effort in this respect has dropped. Before the election, nearly 1.5 per cent of GNP was spent in this country on research and development. Since the election, this percentage has dropped and is now around 1.3 per cent.
My second point is that we must not forget Canada does not provide the same level of support for research and industrial
development as certain competitor countries. A study published in 1986 by the Canadian Manufacturers Association shows that tax support in Canada compares with levels in the United States, Germany, France and England. However, nontax support for research and development lags far behind what is provided in these countries.
As I intend to demonstrate in my speech today, the Government is undermining support measures that work well. I am referring to tax measures instead of increasing non-tax measures to levels comparable to those in other countries. They are trying to undermine tax measures which, as I said before, work very well in this country.
It is a fact that in many other countries, non-tax support takes the form of massive procurement programs, often related to defence or space programs, or, as in Japan, it could be the development of a new generation of computers.
This type of program does not exist in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and that is why we have depended mainly on tax measures to stimulate industrial research, something the Government is once again undermining as a result of its tax reform measures.
The first part of today's motion reads:
(1) tax reform measures that discourage research and development by reducing funds available for R & D, by increasing the costs of R & D and by delaying investment in R & D facilities and delaying the introduction of new products and new processes, all of which generally impair the ability of Canadian companies to compete in global markets;-
Of course, this should be considered in light of the Government's trade initiative, of decreased barriers to international trade and of the need for Canadian firms to be competitive in global markets. Of course, that includes being able to compete right here in Canada in our own domestic market which is but a small part of the larger global market.
In essence, the first part of this motion is the conclusion of a Conference Board survey of some 47 industrial R and D performers which, between them, performed over $1 billion of research and development in 1986. The survey also concluded that the tax reform measures "hold the potential to harm research and development efforts being pursued in their companies and in the economy as a whole".
This survey by the Conference Board was undertaken during the fall of 1987 and was published in December of 1987. It was conducted for the Science Council of Canada which put

May 13, 1988

out a statement at the time of the publication of this report from which I would like to quote. The Science Council believes that some of the proposed tax reforms will be seriously counter-productive in their impact on research and development performing firms. They will penalize the very firms and sectors taking the sorts of risks necessary for Canada to survive in a more competitive world economy and to move with greater confidence into the 21st century. These were the general conclusions of the Conference Board survey and the assessment of the Science Council.
The comments of respondents to the survey showed the extent to which the tax reform measures will damage research and development in Canada on a much more descriptive basis than did the general conclusions that were arrived at by the Conference Board. I would like to quote selectively from the comments contained within this survey. When I say "selectively", that does not mean that I intend to convey only a partial view. I will certainly be quoting from excerpts which I think convey the general thrust of the results of this survey. However, time does not permit me to quote at length from the survey.
There has been a tax reform change on the eligibility of buildings and structures. Buildings and structures are no longer eligible for the 20 per cent investment tax credit. One of the respondents, a large forest products firm, saw a direct impact of this change with both short and long-term consequences. There has been a deferral or cancellation of plans to construct a new research centre which represents an investment of some $15 million to $20 million. That means that $15 million or $20 million has gone down the drain in one forest products company alone.
Similar impacts were expected at a large chemical company, a biotech company, a petroleum firm, and a telecommunications concern. The large chemical company had this to say:
We expect to expand a laboratory next year or in 1989. The abolition of the 100% write-off and the 20% Investment Tax Credit on research buildings will roughly double the cost of this expansion.
The biotech company said that this tax reform measure will affect the ability of the firm to service export markets which likely will be serviced through a facility in those markets rather than in Canada.
The petroleum firm said that a proposed new $46 million research complex in Calgary may not proceed or may be significantly downsized. I do not know if there are any Members from Alberta, from western Canada or from Calgary more particularly in the House at this time, but I am sure they are interested in this petroleum firm in Calgary saying that a $46-million research complex will not proceed or will be significantly downsized.
The telecommunications firm said that the effect of this measure will be, and I quote:
Migration of R & D projects out of Canada over the next few years by large international companies. Cancellation of large long term R & D projects which proposed building new buildings (2-5 years). Reduction of new projects which would involve increased requirement for work space because of losing ITC on base cash-
This survey is full of similar examples which indicate that the tax reform measures proposed and implemented by the Government will have a devastating effect on research and development in Canada, and on the ability of Canadian companies to compete in global markets. If some Members of this House think the survey does not provide conclusive evidence of the damage these tax measures will cause, I refer them to a recent article about Jean de Grandpre, Chairman and outgoing Chief Executive Officer of Bell Canada Enterprises, which appeared in the Report on Business magazine of April, 1988. As the article points out, when economic commentators say that Canada is a world leader in telecommunications, they do not mean Canada, they mean Bell and Northern Telecom. If anyone knows anything about research and development in Canada you would expect the Chairman of Bell Canada Enterprises, owner of the largest research firm in Canada, would know something about it.
I am glad that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) is listening to these comments because Mr. de Grandpre, referring to the Government's plan to eliminate tax deductions for buildings, said: "I told the Deputy Minister, do you think you can do R and D without a roof over your head?" He continued to say that politicians "are all saying the same thing, that we have to have more R and D capacity in Canada, that the future of this country rests on high technology products." However, he says, "The tax reform measures amply demonstrate that politicians don't understand how the game is played. The effect of these tax changes will be that Bell will do its research in some other country and take away several hundred well-paid jobs from Bell Northern Research, the largest private R and D facility in Canada". In what is probably the most devastating comment, he says "Canadians who are graduating from our universities are going to walk over to BNR and say, can I have a job? And we will say, sorry, but we are not expanding our R and D facilities in Canada. They will say, why? Well, because the Government has introduced this stupid piece of legislation."
Here is further evidence of the devastating effect of the Government's tax reform measures. I was at a conference on university research in Edmonton two weeks ago and an official from Connaught Labs revealed that as a result of the tax reform measures, Connaught Labs had to abandon plans to raise $60 million in Canada through an R and D limited partnership. There had been some research developed in Canada at the University of Toronto to come up with an innovative therapy to control diabetes which Connaught Labs wanted to market and further develop here in Canada. The Connaught official said this research work would now be transferred to a large offshore multinational. I referred to this in a question in the House last week and asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to review his tax reform measures. Unfortunately, I did not receive a specific reply to my question.
May 13, 1988

I would now like to refer briefly to the second part of the motion which refers to the management of the investment tax credit for research and development. A survey conducted earlier this year by the Canadian Advanced Technology Association has once again identified serious disagreements between industry and Revenue Canada over the kinds of activity that qualifies for the investment tax credit, and delays of up to 18 months in obtaining refunds. Consequently, many businesses which had been counting on refunds to finance ongoing activities have encountered serious financial difficulties.
One has to put this in context. Very often R and D companies are start-up companies, they are in their first years, short of financing, and they devote every cent they get to ongoing research and development. They are trying to come up with new products to sell here and abroad. They have to devote already limited resources, both financial and people, to justify previous research and development activities rather than concentrating on ongoing R and D. Imagine the situation of some of these companies. They are run by people who are really at home in applying their energy and talents to creating new products. I have spoken to some of them and they told me that they have had to spend an inordinate amount of time dealing with accountants and lawyers trying to justify their previous R and D claims to Revenue Canada rather than concentrating on ongoing research and development activity.
The Government recently made a few changes to its administration of the R and D tax credits which address one aspect of the problem, the tremendous delays incurred by certain companies, proven R and D performers, in obtaining refunds. The extent to which this will apply to new companies, start-up companies, which have new R and D activities remains to be seen. However, none of the changes affected the definition or the possibility of disagreements. Very significant problems remain, once a project is accepted by Revenue Canada, regarding the kinds of costs that you can attribute to a project, such as, for example, overhead, training and travel.
Furthermore, Revenue Canada has been unable to come to grips with companies that develop and sell prototypes. Some tax practitioners have told me that Revenue Canada is simply applying what it perceives to be the current views of the Department of Finance in that it is narrowing what qualifies as R and D. That flies in the face, of course, of all the commitments made by the Government and the Minister of Finance in the past couple of years.
Tax credits are generally supported by industry. They are the favoured form of support in industry because they are self-administered. They are not a program, you do not need to stand in line and apply. Firms choose the type and amount of R and D they want to conduct.
Again, I have been told by a number of tax practitioners that Revenue Canada regards these tax credits very much as a grant program. They want to control the type and amount of
Supply
research and development, which contradicts the very nature of this kind of self-administered program.
I understand that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) will intervene in this debate later today. I want him to state what are the costs of this degree of control. If the administrative costs are higher than the revenues that might be lost if we had less rigorous controls, or if the administrative costs are higher than the kind of revenues that firms would be able to generate by concentrating on R and D rather than spending their time in accounting and legal nightmares, then I suggest the Government really should opt for less rigorous controls. It would make good economic sense. It would only be a matter of common sense to opt for less rigorous controls.
I hope that putting forward this motion today and debating a subject which is often fairly technical and which very often involves the intricacies of the administration of our tax system for which we must rely on the explanations of accountants and lawyers, will advance the debate and indicate to the Government that people in the private sector are seriously concerned about these issues. They will watch the debate today and hopefully we will not hear from the Minister the kind of rhetorical response to which we are accustomed in the House, certainly during Question Period, but a serious attempt will be made to address issues which are of great concern to the private sector.
As I have indicated in my motion, these matters seriously affect research and development in Canada and the ability of Canadian companies to compete in global markets.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate today because it is not only important that the Government explain its record and approach to research and development, but also puts it in the context of tax reform. I invite the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) to consider what I have to say and perhaps we can have a dialogue following my speech.
The motion before the House is one that must be properly considered in the context of tax reform. It must be considered in the context of the benefits of tax reform. As we know, the central objective of tax reform is to lower tax rates because there is no better incentive for growth, investment and job creation than lower tax rates. Lower rates mean that more Canadians keep more of every additional dollar they earn and they, not the Government or accountants, will decide how best to use that money.
How do we lower rates and still have revenue flow to allow a Government to promote and progress further with objectives that are important for the country? This is accomplished by broadening the tax base and reducing the number of tax preferences. That will allow us to lower the rate. Special incentives that remain will be fewer but more effective. They will continue to be sensitive to the needs of Canadians in all parts of the country.

May 13, 1988
Supply

A tax system with lower rates and fewer tax breaks will be fairer for all taxpayers. It will fully reflect our commitment to economic growth and social justice.

The benefits of tax reform will be felt by most Canadians, first through lower personal income taxes, and again over the years as tax reforms have a positive effect on the economy. That is the basic premise of tax reform and that is how it is developing.
In fact, for 9.7 million households, over 85 per cent of the total, tax reform will mean reduced income taxes. The average tax reduction for these households will be about $490 per household. This results from the fact that the gains from tax rate reductions and the conversions of personal exemptions into credits far outweigh the reduction in any tax preferences. Some 850,000 lower-income families, of which about 250,000 are elderly, will have their income tax totally eliminated as a result of tax reform.

Older Canadians who depend mainly on pension and interest income will come out ahead from tax reform. Nine out of ten Canadians aged 65 and over will pay less income tax.

The corporate income tax proposals also present us with a somewhat similar story. They achieve three major objectives. Corporate tax rates, like the personal tax rates, will be reduced. This will promote growth and job creation in Canada by maintaining a corporate tax system that is competitive with other countries, particularly the United States.
Yesterday, I, along with other Members of the House, held very interesting meetings with the Minister of Finance of New Zealand. The Labour Government there has unleashed very strong economic growth through a number of programs, including privatization and freer trade, as well as by reducing corporate tax rates. It has resulted in unprecedented economic growth in New Zealand.
That is our strategy for the corporate tax structure as well as the personal tax structure. The elimination or reduction of many special tax breaks on the corporate side will pay for lower corporate and personal tax rates and will return the profit motive to investment by rewarding success. It will encourage investment decisions based more on economic initiative and opportunity than on tax considerations. That is the key.
The Hon. Member for Laurier was curiously old-fashioned in his remarks. He wants us to return to the 1960s and 1970s when incentives were distorted so that people focused on obtaining some sort of tax preference or loophole to make an investment decision. That is not the way to run a corporate tax system. We have tried to prune the system of these preferences and lower the rates.
A broader tax base with fewer preferences will mean that profitable corporations will pay a bigger share of the corporate tax burden and the corporate income tax will be a more predictable and reliable source of revenue.
Throughout the entire economy, corporate tax reform will strengthen incentive for firms to invest in profitable ventures. The rate of tax and the return for new investment will be reduced and the tax treatment of capital in this country will continue to encourage risk taking, initiative, growth and job creation.
The Hon. Member for Laurier stated that the Government is not doing enough in this context to support research and development in Canada. My colleague will refute this later this morning with respect to non-tax support for R and D. He will go through the support for R and D brought forward by this Government on the non-tax side. I will refute this with respect to tax reform and the tax treatment of R and D generally.
I am disappointed that the substantial support in fact provided by research and development tax credits is not fully recognized by the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger). In 1986, for example, over $700 million of R and D tax credits were generated by R and D companies. This is a very significant level of commitment in the face of competing fiscal pressures. This Government has many fiscal pressures, and that is a large level of tax credits compared to any other activity of the Government.

This Government is committed to promoting science and technology in Canada. I am surprised to see the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) trying to create a negative perception of our tax incentives for research and development.

Tax reform generally represented a move to a more results-based corporate income tax system featuring broader based incentives provided through lower tax rates. In general, there is an elimination or reduction of selective up-front deductions or credits. That is what tax reform did in general. It tried to eliminate these very selective up-front deductions so that incentives could be delivered, as I have said, through a reduced rate.
However, incentives were retained, and the Hon. Member knows this, in certain strategic areas. Tax reform recognized the importance of R and D to the economic future of the country. That was one of the strategic areas. In fact, Canada continues to offer the most generous package of R and D tax incentives among the major industrialized countries. The OECD did a study, which I examined six months ago, which ranked the Canadian tax approach to R and D very, very, highly as a very generous system. We have retained that even with tax reform.
May 13, 1988

For example, the United States only provides credits for increases in R and D spending-the Hon. Member for Laurier should consult what the Americans do-while the Canadian system provides credits for all of R and D spending, not just the increases. This fact is widely acknowledged and applauded by the R and D community.
Does the Hon. Member object to this? This is a very generous approach. This is more important than loose interpretations of R and D. More important than that is to provide credit for all of these expenditures. Because of our commitment to science and technology, these generous R and D incentives were maintained. We maintained them because of our commitment to it. For the most part, following tax reform, we maintained this notwithstanding the reduction or elimination of many other incentives.
The Hon. Member's approach is a bit different. He in fact wants loose interpretation of rules, probably to bring back the scientific research tax credit approach which cost the Canadian people billions and billions of dollars. As far as anyone can tell, it promoted almost no research and development at all. That approach is to construct a great wide-open door-put research and development inside and people drive trucks through it. In fact no research is being done at all, but you get the tax benefit for it. What we have done is to maintain the special status of R and D, but we want it to be R and D.

In fact, despite what the Hon. Member for Laurier said, tax reform has indeed increased the effect of the main tax provisions for research and development.

For example, the rates of the R and D investment tax credits were maintained following tax reform notwithstanding the fact that the general and regional ITCs are being eliminated or reduced to reflect reduced tax rates. By maintaining the rates of the R and D ITCs, while reducing tax rates, the relative benefit of these tax credits is increased. The same level of R and D will now entitle the R and D performer to credits which will offset the tax on more income. This enhances the incentive impact of our R and D provisions.
I ask the Hon. Member for Laurier, does he not approve of that? Does he object to that? It is very generous and a very, very important part of how our ITCs work in Canada.
Changes were made to the R and D tax incentives to ensure that as a package they operate in an efficient and cost-effective manner which is consistent with other government priorities. We want things to be efficient and effective. We do not want simply labels that say R and D, through which tax reductions are received but through which very little R and D is done.
As the Hon. Member knows, as part of the tax reform changes, expenditures made for the acquisition of a building will no longer qualify for the R and D tax incentives. The Hon. Member mentioned this. Buildings normally depreciate slowly over time, if at all, and they have very long, useful lives. They
Supply
are eligible for debt financing, which is not generally available for more direct R and D expenditures. Accordingly, a 100 per cent immediate write-off in the R and D ITC was considered to be inappropriate in a post-tax reform environment. Is that what the Hon. Member wants? Does he want to neglect those realities? By excluding these expenditures, the tax treatment for R and D buildings in Canada will be more in line with that found in the other major industrialized countries, and the high rate of ITC could be maintained for other R and D expenditures.
The final tax reform package also provides that investment tax credits cannot offset, in general, more than three-quarters of a corporation's tax otherwise payable. The introduction of limits to the amount of ITC which a taxpayer may claim in a year is an important part of the tax reform package. It improves the fairness of the system by ensuring that large profitable corporations pay at least some tax, including those corporations that perform R and D. Corporations that perform R and D should pay some tax. Part of tax reform is to restore to our system a sense of fairness across industrialized groups. We have had some industrialized groups, for example, the real estate sector and the financial institutions sector. The R and D sector has to be part of it. They should pay some tax. Tax reform allows for that.
This limit was originally set at 50 per cent of a large corporation's federal tax liability for a year. However, consultations with industry indicated that this limit would have a greater impact on R and D-intensive sectors than was originally anticipated. Accordingly, the Government reacted and this limit was increased from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of a large corporation's federal tax liability. To be sensitive to what that sector is saying was very important to us. We listened and we increased the limit.

It will help strike a better balance between the need to encourage research and development, on one hand, and the assurance that large profitable corporations indeed pay income tax, on the other hand.

The tax credit limitation is in line, in fact, with tax law in the United States, where the general business credit, which includes the U.S. research credit, is subject to a tax credit claiming limitation of 75 per cent of tax liability over $25,000.
Over the last few days we have had questions in the House about corporations not paying tax. The opposition Members complain that a number of corporations do not pay tax. We are trying to ensure that corporations do pay tax, and the Hon. Member is criticizing that.
These limits may have some impact, I have admitted, on ITCs earned before tax reform and carried forward. It is important to note that ITCs earned before tax reform were

May 13, 1988
Supply
earned when tax rates were higher. With the reduction in tax rates resulting from tax reform, existing banks of unused ITCs can now offset a tax on a greater amount of taxable income. Most accountants know that. I encourage the Elon. Member for Laurier, who has been talking to his accountant and hearing these complaints, to ensure that his accountant knows this. From a tax theory perspective, these existing banks of ITCs could have been reduced to reflect these lower tax rates with some justification. Indeed, this was the approach taken in the U.S. tax reform.
In Canada, however, this approach was not taken. Instead, the introduction of the ITC limits obviates the need for such a reduction. The ITC limits also better serve the competing objectives of providing the maximum incentive of R and D through the tax system and ensuring that the tax system is fair and is perceived to be fair by ordinary Canadians. That is how we make it fair. That is how we ensure that people feel it is fair, to limit the amount of these credits, to ensure that corporations across Canada all pay tax.
The final tax reform proposals also contain changes to the Income Tax Act designed to prevent the syndication of R and D incentives through limited partnerships and similar arrangements. When these federal R and D incentives were first introduced, they were intended to be available to R and D performers only. They were designed to have some relationship to the taxpayers' business rather than be a tax shelter flow-out mechanism. We do not want everyone in Canada trying to protect their income by trying to identify some R and D that is really not R and D. What we wanted to do was to encourage the solid R and D performers. We have done that.
In response to flow-out strategies which were developing at the time, the disastrous scientific research tax credit mechanism was introduced by the Liberal Government in 1983. This was disastrous for reasons with which the House is very familiar. It did not work. It produced very little R and D. Billions of dollars worth of revenue were lost to the Canadian Government. With the repeal of this mechanism in 1985 by this Government and its replacement with the refundability features of the R and D investment tax credits, the expressed policy of this Government was that R and D incentives be used by the R and D performer itself, not as a flow-out mechanism to somebody else.
We recognize that no matter how generous the R and D ITCs might be, they would not provide sufficient incentives to those small and start-up R and D companies which may have little or no taxable income and therefore no tax to offset through tax credits.
What did we do in this case for the small R and D performers? Accordingly, for small corporations the enhanced 35 per cent tax credit available in respect of the first $2 million of R and D expenditures of a current nature was made fully refundable. In effect, this provides a direct payment of up to $700,000 per year for eligible corporations.
Allowing R and D tax incentives to be transferred to passive investors at this time would be particularly inappropriate in view of the Government's tax reform philosophy and approach. We have improved the fairness of the system. We have had to do this by eliminating more and more flow-out shelters. For these reasons the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced amendments to the Income Tax Act on December 16, 1987, relating to R and D incentives. These amendments will have the effect of preventing the flow-out for federal tax purposes of R and D incentives to passive investors. Instead, it is important that steps be taken to ensure that the refundable R and D ITC program works well and provides refunds to small and start-up corporations on a timely basis.
Since 1985, this part of the R and D tax credit program has already provided a cumulative stimulus for R and D of more than $1 billion. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue (Mrs. Mailly) will be explaining this.
The Government has taken a number of important steps to ensure that funds are delivered to qualifying claimants through this program on an expeditious basis. The Hon. Member wants an "open sesame" in interpretations. That is not what the Canadian people want. What they would like is expeditious processing of requests. These changes accomplish two objectives. They will ensure that companies with a proven track record in R and D do not experience administrative delay. First, they will also permit Revenue Canada to concentrate greater efforts on validating the refund claims of first-time claimants in a shorter period of time. That is very good news.
A great deal of credit for improvements in this program since its introduction must go to Canadian industry. Revenue Canada received excellent advice directly from the industry and through its technical liaison committee.

These changes will considerably improve the operation of this important program.

In conclusion I take the view that this Government's support for R and D, both directly and through the tax system, is and continues to be substantial. The record of billions of dollars of investment for R and D is there to prove it.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister for his contribution. I feel that the debate today in the House will advance the debate in the country. It will certainly allow people to understand the opposing philosophies that are being put forward by the Government and by our Party.
The Minister said that the question of R and D tax incentives has to be considered in the context of over-all tax reform. I can tell him that I have serious questions about tying ourselves to tax reform measures in the United States, which has not had a great record in innovation in recent years and in competing with other countries where approaches may be somewhat different.
May 13, 1988

I think that he has to look at the matter in the context of what his leader said a few years ago. He said that R and D is the lifeblood of a successful company. He has to consider it in light of the fact that Canada's performance in R and D is half of what occurs in other countries. Our industrial research and development activities are anaemic. Only 2 per cent to 3 per cent of firms in Canada whose future depends on technology do any R and D.
He said that our tax system was very generous. It is equivalent to that of our major competitors, as I indicated by referring to a study by the Canadian Manufacturers Association. Where we are really deficient is in non-tax support, where we are not even in the same league as the United States, France or Japan.
What I suggest that his Government is doing now is, rather than beefing up the non-tax support, reducing the support in the tax system which is the only type of support that is available to industrial R and D performers in Canada.
Regarding the assertion that I am asking for a loose interpretation of the rules and that the SRTC be brought back, at no time did I suggest during my comments that we should bring back the SRTC. The current R and D tax credit program is a horse of a different colour. R and D has to be performed before a refund is applied for, which is far different from the SRTC mechanism.
What I suggested to him, and I make the suggestion again, is that there is an obligation on the part of the Government to tell us what are the costs of the degree of control that the Government is exerting at the present time. Gordon McNab, the head of Pre-Carn a pre-competitive R and D consortium which is in the course of being established, said in Edmonton a couple of weeks ago that the current philosophy in Revenue Canada is that one is guilty until proven innocent. What are the costs of this degree of control? Not just direct costs but the opportunity costs.
I put it to the Minister again that if administrative costs are higher than the revenues that would be lost if we had less rigorous controls or less restrictive interpretations, and if firms are able to generate greater revenues by concentrating on research and development, then the Government should opt for a more expansive definition and less rigorous controls.

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the comments made by the Hon. Member for Laurier. I am not too sure whether there are any questions in his comments, but I will take his comments and reformulate them into a question, one which I think he is putting to me.
He is saying that we have simply tightened the tax provisions for R and D and therefore we are against R and D. I think that is the burden of his argument and the burden of his comments of a moment ago. In fact, what we have done is to
have lowered the rate of corporate tax generally. He forgets that. That is very good news for anybody investing in R and D, and anybody aiming for profitability.
Second, we have made a number of important improvements since the Budget of 1985. I mentioned in my speech the change that we brought about to ITCs-

subsubtopic: SUGAR-BEET PRODUCERS-INTERIM PAYMENT UNDER STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's sugar-beet producers will soon receive an interim stabilization payment from the National Tripartite Price Stabilization Program. The interim payment, amounting to $6 per field tonne, will be paid to 970 eligible producers in Manitoba and Alberta by the end of May.
In total, some $6 million will be paid out. The federal Government will advance $4.3 million to make this interim payment possible.
In spite of opposition from the former New Democratic Government of Manitoba, a sugar-beet tripartite plan is now in place. The establishment of that plan has allowed for this needed interim payment, and shows the federal Government's commitment to specialized Canadian agriculture.
The former New Democratic Government of Manitoba showed no commitment. This is why it is the "former" Government.
New Democrats, both provincially and federally, have never understood Canadian agriculture.

subtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR-POWERED SUBMARINES- CALL FOR PUBLIC ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR-POWERED SUBMARINES- CALL FOR PUBLIC ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are many compelling arguments against the Government's proposal to purchase nuclear-powered submarines. This week the Canadian Environment Network added yet another, pointing out that nuclear powered submarines are floating nuclear reactors in the fragile Arctic environment.

May 13, 1988
We therefore urge the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) to launch a public environmental assessment of the proposed nuclear powered submarines.
While this is important, there are at least two more urgent priorities: a real, national, first-class day care program for the next generation, and the badly needed sewage and water treatment program proposed by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities.
Canadians, Mr. Speaker, want basics, and not the "Beatty" nuclear power trip.

subtopic: QUEBEC MINISTER OF FINANCE CONGRATULATED ON BUDGET

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: QUEBEC MINISTER OF FINANCE CONGRATULATED ON BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we want to pay tribute to the Government of Quebec and Minister of Finance (Mr. Levesque) for the excellent Budget he has just unveiled: lower taxes, reduced deficit, expenditure control, and harmonization of provincial and federal tax measures.
The current economic upsurge called for lower expenditures and taxes in preparation for more difficult years. The Government of Quebec did act in light of this economic tenet. Unfortunately, in a very similar context the Liberal Government of Ontario ignored this economic precept and increased both expenditures and taxes. Congratulations to the Government of Quebec!

Mr. Speaker, higher postal rates are to take effect in January, with the cost of mailing a standard letter going from 37 cents to 38 cents.
While rates will go up for all Canadians, some Canadians are suffering cut-backs in service. For example, those buying a new home in a suburban area of Canada, such as Port Moody, Port Coquitlam, or Coquitlam in British Columbia, will get their mail from a supermailbox, while their fellow citizens get door-to-door delivery.
This is not fair. My Leader, the Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), and I recently met with the Mayor and Councillors of Port Moody on this issue. We visited a "Mulroney" mailbox in the area.
Order!

1 attended public hearings in Port Coquitlam on this issue, and I learned that supermailboxes cause litter, lower property values, and result in traffic that is dangerous to young children, in addition to providing a lesser level of service.
Supermailboxes should be removed. The Post Office should be a public service, not a money-making machine. Canadians must be treated fairly and equally.
This is going to be an issue in the upcoming election.

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF NEW DOCUMENTARY ON BILLY BISHOP, V.C.
PRODUCTION OF NEW DOCUMENTARY ON BILLY BISHOP, V.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's National Film Board has finally found a producer to take on its promised new feature documentary on Billy Bishop.
The previous so-called documentary on Billy Bishop, "The Kid Who Couldn't Miss", was bitterly condemned by Canadians in all walks of life for defaming the legendary World War I Canadian hero.
The producer of the new film, George Pearson, wants firm guarantees of further extensive research into all aspects of Bishop's life before proceeding with the film. This would include information from books personally written by Bishop and his son, and from all other sources.
I believe Mr. Pearson should have these guarantees, Mr. Speaker, because I do not think the public would be satisfied with anything less, and we could thus ensure that the entire production of the film would be based entirely on facts that can be substantiated.
I do not believe that Canadians across Canada would accept anything less, nor would Billy Bishop. So, let's get on with the film.

Mr. Speaker, Canada Post has just announced its five-year plan, indicating that revenues are expected to increase and that it will again charge more for postage stamps.
Will we be paying more for postage in exchange for more services, Mr. Speaker? No way! As a matter of fact the number of so-called superboxes-for those who are not aware of this, superboxes mean reduced services-will rise from
232,000	to 340,000.
May 13, 1988

Mr. Speaker, people who live in Glengarry-Prescott- Russell, Orleans and others elsewhere in the National Capital Region simply do not want to have anything more to do with the Prime Minister's superboxes. What they want is home delivery. Nothing less is acceptable!

Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the Hon. Marcel Masse, Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and the Hon. Gerald Merrithew, Minister of State for Forestry and Mines, on the introduction of the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program, an initiative that has been exceptionally well received by the Canadian mining and petroleum industries.
The program is designed to assist junior mining and oil and gas exploration companies in raising equity in the marketplace, in addition to contributing to regional economic development in Canada.
Mining is a major industry, directly employing about
105,000	Canadians. Closely related downstream industries employ another 230,000 Canadians.
The Exploration Incentive Program will provide for more than 12,000 person-years of employment, and will contribute to Canada's economic development.
In addition, the mining industry produces a market for high technology goods and services. It is more than 70 per cent Canadian owned. Early indications are that the free trade arrangement will result in Canadian mining companies increasing their ownership in the American mining industry.
This incentive program, Mr. Speaker, is good for the Canadian mining industry. It is good for the regions, and it is good for Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PREMIER'S COMMENT ON CARE OF HUNGRY CHILDREN
BRITISH COLUMBIA-PREMIER'S COMMENT ON CARE OF HUNGRY CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again B.C. Premier Vander Zalm has shown his ignorance and insensitivity when it comes to poor kids and their families. He suggested that children who go to school hungry have parents who do not love them enough; that if they do not have lunches, it is because "their parents lay in bed, not really caring".
Such a callous attitude by B.C.'s First Minister must cause real despair and anguish among the thousands of British
Columbia parents who live in poverty and have to watch their children grow up in poverty.
These parents already know the impossibility of trying to stretch inadequate welfare cheques into the last week of the month so that they can pay the rent while at the same time providing their children with decent food.
Children constitute the fastest growing poverty group in Canada. Instead of blaming the parents, Mr. Vander Zalm should look to himself.
The Premier and his Government have said "no" to school lunch programs; the Premier and his Government tried to cut welfare rates for single mothers.
Premier Vander Zalm's heart must be very small and very cold. It seems there is no room in his heart for hungry children.

subtopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-CMHC EXPENDITURES ON SOCIAL HOUSING PROJECTS
NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-CMHC EXPENDITURES ON SOCIAL HOUSING PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently opposition Members have been criticizing the Government for not doing enough for housing in remote areas.
In respect of the Northwest Territories this accusation is categorically false.
In 1987, apart from insuring over $60 million worth of mortgage loans, CMHC spent some $48 million on social housing projects in the Territories, amounting to nearly $1,000 for every man, woman, and child. Included was some $15 million for 214 Homeowner Assistance Program houses, amounting to an outright grant of over $70,000 for each unit.
This is not miserliness, Mr. Speaker; this is generosity- almost to the point of abandon.

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO DERIVE INSPIRATION FROM QUEBEC SOCIAL MEASURES
OPPORTUNITY TO DERIVE INSPIRATION FROM QUEBEC SOCIAL MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to know why this Conservative Government does not follow the example set yesterday by the Bourassa Government's Budget on family matters. Yesterday, the Bourassa Government recognized the importance of families and children with a $500 tax credit on the first two children, while this Conservative Government only provides for a meagre $65. Moreover, for a third child the Bourassa Government introduces a $3,000 tax credit, while the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) Conservative Government only provides for a meagre $130, Mr. Speaker.

May 13, 1988
Moreover, the Liberal Government extends a tax exemption on family allowance, while this Conservative Government deindexes family allowance. Mr. Robert Bourassa's Liberal Government is granting $60,000 for child care services in Quebec, while this Conservative Government does nothing for those people. While Mr. Bourassa's Liberal Government brought in a $772 million tax reduction for families, this Conservative Government has brought in increases, Mr. Speaker.
Why is this Conservative Government not following the example set by a good Liberal Government?

subtopic: INDUSTRY'S CONTRIBUTION TO GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
INDUSTRY'S CONTRIBUTION TO GROSS NATIONAL PRODUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next week marks a very important one for Canadians. It is National Tourism Week which recognizes one of this country's fastest growing industries.
Tourism employs over 600,000 Canadians. That is more than mining, forestry or agriculture. It generates over $20 billion in revenue and contributes 4.5 per cent to the Gross National Product. In addition it is the third largest industry. Tourism is not only big business, it is every Canadian's business.
Canada and Canadians have a great deal to offer visitors, our distinct culture, our unique heritage and, of course, our beautiful country.
I hope that Hon. Members and all Canadians will take the opportunity to help observe a week which symbolizes one of Canada's most important industries, tourism.

Mr. Speaker, next week is Tourism Awareness Week. The tourist industry employs
600,000	and is a $20 billion industry in Canada. Each year foreign visitors who come to Canada, we hope are welcomed with open arms.
In an effort to promote a good image for Canadian tourism, most of the chartered banks cashed travellers cheques without
charge during Expo 86. But since then, with the exception only of the Bank of Montreal, the banks are levying a substantial service charge to cash travellers cheques. There has been a great deal of protest from private citizens and small business alike over this move.
Tourism plays a vitally important role in our economy. Let the banks do their part. I encourage these financial institutions to reinstate their 1986 policy, and let foreign travellers and Canadians alike know that we welcome tourists in our country.

Mr. Speaker, over the week-end the Liberals are holding their fund-raising brunch. According to their so-called Quebec Leader, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), there should be 1,000 guests. How do they get them, Mr. Speaker? In my constituency, they are giving away the $300 per person tickets for that brunch and there is some arm-twisting going on to get people to attend. Is that what they call democratic funding? What does that prove, giving tickets away? Mr. Speaker, is that good management? Can Canadians trust a Party that sank us into debt through mismanagement?
That reminds us of the penitentiary!
They are a conniving brunch!

Yes, that is it just like a conniving party!
Mr. Speaker, their leader is paying $300 per person to listen to him. Is that showing leadership and unity? How much is an unwanted leader costing the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, the Mila melee has reached hyperbolic proportions. We hear the Chairman of the Quebec caucus of the Progressive Conservatives now comparing Canada to South Africa because of an unfortunate incident.
May 13, 1988

I think all Canadians were very disappointed and discouraged with what happened in Moncton those few short days ago, but I think once again the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) does not know when to cut the rhetoric, and when to recognize that an incident which should have been avoided and was not has turned into a political disaster for himself and his Party. Ele has had the Minister from the province telegram and suggest somehow that the labour movement was involved in inciting violence. He has now suggested in a speech to students that we should have an end to "brutality", but the hype had to be when the Chairman of the Quebec caucus compared Canada to South Africa.
It is ridiculous. It is outrageous. Let's have an end to the Mila melee.

[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, the coming agreement between the Quebec Government and the Canadian Government on the St. Lawrence River clean-up and on the establishment of a marine national park in the Saguenay fjord is sparking a lot of interest. The enactment of Bill C-74, the Environmental Protection Act, is raising a lot of hope among all Canadians. All my fellow citizens have asked me to ask the Liberal dominated Canadian Senate to pass that extremely progressive bill, which is the most advanced in any western country, as soon as possible. For the first time indeed a federal statute includes a definition of the term "environment", Mr. Speaker. The definition of "toxic substances" now provides for protection at three levels-protection of the environment as such; protection of the environment as it interacts with human life; health protection for Canadians. Chemical substances also will be controlled at every stage of their life cycle, that is from either import or research and development to final disposal, through manufacturing, transport, distribution and use. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, in order to be really effective, it provides for strict penalties against offenders. Serious offences under the Act can now lead to charges under the Criminal Code, and the maximum penalty provided for is life emprison-ment.

Mr. Speaker, other countries are responding to research trends showing that the harm of even low level exposure to radiation
Oral Questions
has been underestimated. Other countries are bringing in tougher standards. Canada should be doing the same, yet a report of the International Institute for Concerns for Public Health suggests that Health and Welfare Canada is trying to raise the allowable level of cesium 137 by more than tenfold.
Radioactive fallout from the Chernobyl accident and from nuclear weapons testing in the 1950s and 1960s is particularly harmful in the far north. The caribou are contaminated by the lichen and the Inuit eat the caribou. If the new weaker standards are accepted, this will legitimize the federal Government's practice of not warning the Inuit or protecting them, yet cesium 137 is responsible for cancer deaths, birth defects, genetic damage, and a weakening of the immune system.
We need a public process to ensure that adequate standards are set and maintained. The federal Government must not be allowed to get away with this dereliction of duty.

In 1984, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party had a great project: create jobs, set the country on a sound financial base, establish good relations with the provinces, tighten our ties with other countries, improve national security, and attract investors to Canada.
This great project has now become reality: we did create more than 1,200,000 jobs since our election, business is flourishing, and Canadian men and women stand prouder and have renewed faith in their future. Canadians, Quebecers and the people of Longueuil feel better and live more comfortably with our Party.

subsubtopic: SUPERMAILBOXES-PROJECTED INCREASE IN NUMBERS
speechtext:

In 1981-82 the deficit was $588 million when the hon. gentlemen opposite were in the middle of their wasteful and profligate careers in the Government of Canada.

subtopic: INSTALLATION OF SUPERMAILBOXES IN RURAL AREAS
INSTALLATION OF SUPERMAILBOXES IN RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister must be blind, deaf, and dumb to the complaints of Canadians. We received another one just yesterday. If a person mails a letter in one of the supermailbox slots after 11 a.m. on Friday, it will remain there all day Friday, all day Saturday, all day Sunday, to a minimum of Monday, unless it is a holiday and then it is not picked up until Tuesday. This Government dares to brag about improvements in service.
One of the places that Canada Post will pepper with supermailboxes is rural Canada. How can the Cabinet now condone the continuation of Canada Post's 10-year plan totally to eradicate post offices in rural Canada, 5,221 of them that will close? How can he condone the replacement of many of these rural post offices with these infamous supermailboxes?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: INSTALLATION OF SUPERMAILBOXES IN RURAL AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is, of course, no such plan to eradicate rural post offices totally. There is a plan for the steady improvement of rural post office service and that plan is under way now. The supermailbox that the hon. gentleman seems not
to be in favour of is, by many people, found to be very helpful in the postal system.
I might point out to the hon. gentleman that if we had door-to-door delivery for all Canadians, this would mean that we would need to have a 60-cent stamp. While I know that that does not shock the hon. gentleman opposite, most Canadians do not want to see a 60-cent postal stamp.
I might finish by saying that the hon. gentleman froths at the gills about fish, and now he is frothing at the gills about the Post Office. He should cease frothing and relax.

Mr. Speaker, in the past four years we have seen our postal service disintegrate to the point where many urban Canadians are no longer receiving door-to-door delivery, where all rural Canadians have lost or will lose their traditional post offices as they knew them, where mail now takes longer than ever before to be delivered, where loss and damage of mail are on an alarming increase, all due to the policies of this Tory Government. Does the Minister not think that, instead of bragging about black ink in the House today, we should be hanging out black crepe to mourn the loss of the postal service in Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman opposite will obviously be black and blue if he continues with such a silly line of questions. He says that he wants to continue the traditional post office. The traditional post office, a hundred years ago, had a spittoon in the corner. Is he insisting that we continue the spittoon regime, or should we not move into the 21st century which is the direction we are moving in, and give a better service at a lower cost?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLEGED USE OF GOVERNMENT HELICOPTERS BY LUCIEN BOUCHARD
speechtext:
In the same line of thought, Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the Conservative Party has jumped ahead into the 21st century!
Last April 29, Lucien Bouchard landed at the Alma airport on his way to announce he would be running as Progressive Conservative Party candidate in the Lac-Saint-Jean riding. But like prophet Elias who rode down from the sky in his chariot of fire, he boarded a Transport Canada helicopter to travel the short distance between the airport and downtown Alma.
May 13, 1988

I want to ask the Government why a Government helicopter was used to such partisan ends? How much did such unwarranted luxury cost the taxpayers? And how many more abuses will the Government tolerate in an attempt to have the Prime Minister's school chum elected?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED USE OF GOVERNMENT HELICOPTERS BY LUCIEN BOUCHARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one has to be grasping at straws to come up with this kind of silly questions. As far as I know, on April 29 the Secretary of State did not fly in a Transport Canada helicopter to go from the Alma airport to I do not know where, for the simple reason Mr. Speaker, that Alma is not Montreal and therefore it is faster to use a car to travel around.
I think my colleague has been badly advised, and we are in for a very long election campaign if they always come up with this kind of information. I would suggest you deal with more serious issues, please!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is that the Minister has never heard that the other number one Minister used a helicopter on his way to announce his candidacy as a Tory candidate in the Lac-Saint-Jean riding. I would like to ask the Minister to double-check and to provide us with the information as to whether or not such a helicopter, owned and operated by Transport Canada, took the Minister from the airport to Alma, and how much it cost. I would like the Minister to double-check on that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to be very serious. I cannot understand that a serious Party could raise that kind of misleading information about Mr. Bouchard and the assessment that he could use a Transport Canada helicopter.
I am the Minister of Transport and I am not even aware that we have any helicopters with Transport Canada in Lac-Saint-Jean. The helicopters belong to the Department of National Defence and they are based in Bagotville. There is not any way that Mr. Lucien Bouchard used them.
Once again, it is unbelievable that we can advance any kind of information when the Party opposite is not even able to find a candidate in Lac-Saint-Jean. I do not understand. If you want to be political, do it properly, please.

subsubtopic: CHALLENGES OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Finance and it concerns the loopholes in the minimum tax that have enabled
Oral Questions
more than 5,000 Canadians with good incomes to avoid paying any income tax in 1986.
This week, the Minister of Finance challenged my Party to tell him how the minimum tax should be strengthened. My answer to this challenge is: Why have the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State and the Government ignored the suggestions that New Democrats have put forward to eliminate the loopholes in the minimum tax?
I challenge the Minister: Is the Government now prepared to take the New Democrats' suggestion to strengthen the minimum tax by including all capital gains that are not affected thanks to the $100,000 exemption and by including the excessive financial costs used in calculating the minimum tax? Or do you intend to maintain a minimum tax that is both ineffective and unfair?

subsubtopic: CHALLENGES OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows that we have eliminated many loopholes. What have we done with the money? With it, we have improved the spouse's allowance and the refundable sales tax credit, increased the child tax credit, provided advanced payments for the child tax credit, increased services for the disabled, etc. That is what we have done with the money from all the loopholes that we have eliminated.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Minister has forgotten that in 1984 Canadians wanted fairness from the tax system. One of the things they felt they were promised by the Prime Minister was a minimum tax that would ensure that wealthy Canadians paid their share of income tax.
Does the Minister recall that the Finance Department itself estimated back in 1985 that three out of four of those upper-income Canadians who were avoiding paying any income tax at all would be caught by the minimum tax? Does the Minister of State for Finance think it is fair that only one-third of those wealthy Canadians who were not paying tax have been caught by the minimum tax? Is the Minister prepared to take the NDP's challenge to come up with new additions to the minimum tax that will ensure that it is fair and that it makes wealthy Canadians pay?

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago in the House the Minister of Finance explained the tremendous progress we have made in terms of getting high-income individuals who paid no tax to pay tax. The number of high-income individuals who paid no tax declined significantly between 1985 and 1986.
In 1985 the number of those with incomes of $50,000 or more and who paid no tax was 7,947. In 1986 it was 5,220, a decrease of 34 per cent. Those with an income over $250,000 who paid no tax went from 254 to 40, an 84 per cent decrease.

May 13, 1988
Oral Questions
Why are there still a few high-income Canadians who pay no taxes? The Hon. Member knows why-medical disability expenses, alimony expenses, charitable contributions, union dues. Is the Hon. Member saying he wants to do away with the deduction for union dues, or alimony, or medical disability payments?

Mr. Speaker, let us talk about the 40 high-income Canadians, the top 40 on the Minister of Finance's list, who had income over $250,000 in 1986 and did not pay a dime of income tax. That is not a group which has to pay union dues. That is not a group with a significant amount of alimony to pay.
How do you know?

We have checked the figures with Revenue Canada. What we do know is that almost three-quarters of those wealthy Canadians had carrying charges amounting to an average of $227,000 apiece. That is how they were able to bring their income tax down to zero. 1 will repeat that since the Minister looks a bit surprised. Twenty-nine of those 40 wealthy Canadians had carrying charges amounting to an average of $227,000 apiece. That is how they were able to bring their income tax down to zero.

Mr. Speaker, will the Minister accept the NDP's challenge to bring in a minimum tax which is fair and just? Will the Government act so that where interest costs exceed a person's investment income, that is where there are excessive carrying charges, that loophole cannot be used by wealthy Canadians as a way of avoiding paying the minimum tax? Will he move on that now?

Mr. Speaker, I noticed a few months ago that the NDP changed its view on a major tax deduction, flow-through shares. This Party has always believed in flow-through shares because of what they meant for northern Quebec and Ontario and the development of the mineral industry in Canada. His Party totally flip-flopped on this issue. Deductions for flow-through shares can put you in a position where your tax liability is greatly reduced or eliminated. The NDP is now in favour of this, and maybe that is the reason why there are still a few who will not be paying taxes.

Mr. Speaker, the Tories are jeopardizing the future of the French
language in Canada. According to the Gens de I'air, French is downgraded by Air Canada; a study made by the Quebec Government indicates that French-speaking athletes are neglected at international events and the fact that a coalition has been formed to promote French at Radio-Canada are additional proof that such is the case; the French language network of the CBC is seriously affected. The Coalition for the defence of the French language services in the CBC has denounced the discrimination shown against the French network where budgets are reduced while those of the English network are increasing. As an example, the Coalition draws attention to a program Le Point, a program whose budget is much lower than that earmarked for The Journal of the CBC.
My question to the the acting Minister of Communications is as follows: Is the government ready to accept the recommendations made by the Coalition: 1. That the specific character and special needs of the French language network be recognized and 2: That the budget provided by Government to the French language network of the CBC be discussed and adopted separately from those granted to the English language network?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Communications is absent today and I am trying to fill in for her, and that is certainly difficult. The answer to the hon. gentleman's question of course is that the way in which the CBC allocates its budget among various priorities is a decision for the CBC and not the Government. Member that the Minister is aware of and certainly supports the importance of the distinctive character of French-language broadcasting and this will be reflected in the new broadcasting legislation.

subtopic: RECOMMENDATIONS MADE BY COALITION FOR DEFENCE OF RADIO-CANADA'S FRENCH SERVICE-MINISTER'S POSITION

Minister to get involved in Radio-Canada's affairs, but to exercise his own and his government's authority.

subtopic: BY-ELECTIONS NUMBER OF OFFICES AT EXCLUSIVE SERVICE OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE IN LAC-SAINT-JEAN

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BY-ELECTIONS NUMBER OF OFFICES AT EXCLUSIVE SERVICE OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE IN LAC-SAINT-JEAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Government. I would like to get back to the by-election in the riding of Lac-Saint-Jean and the ministerial candidate who, after being temporarily parachuted into the riding via helicopter, will pick up his toys the day after the election and go play in his own backyard. It seems there are four offices in the riding, paid for with taxpayers money: two in Alma, one in Chicoutimi North, and a fourth office will open in Jonquiere on June 6, and this is not counting the candidate's election office.
I want to ask the Minister how many offices this Conservative candidate needs to "fix" his election?

subtopic: BY-ELECTIONS NUMBER OF OFFICES AT EXCLUSIVE SERVICE OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE IN LAC-SAINT-JEAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question is extremely partisan. However, I realize that considering the Hon. Member's situation . .. Mr. Speaker there are two offices. One, an office of the Department of the Secretary of State, operates in Alma, with someone from the Department to respond to requests made in connection with Mr. Lucien Bouchard's function as Canada's Secretary of State. I think this is just a matter of providing a service to Canadians, which is normal. There is another office-all candidates have one in every election-to take care of the political side. We have said it before and we say it again, and, I think we can hardly accuse the Chief Electoral Officer of being partisan, that even he has stated he was aware of the situation and that operating expenditures for this office have no impact at all on election spending.
I think the Hon. Member is well aware of that. Canadians realize that there is an administrative side as well. Canadians are entitled to receive services from the Department of the Secretary of State and the Secretary of State, and they get those services and have access to them. The people of Lac-Saint-Jean are entitled to have a political office operated on behalf of a Conservative candidate, and I think the two are completely separate, and there is no connection between the two offices.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two other offices, constituency offices. I mentioned them in my previous question. One is in Chicoutimi North and one is in Alma. That makes five offices if one counts the election office of the candidate.
I want to repeat my question because it is very important. Four of those offices are paid for by public funds, voted for by this House. How many offices does Mr. Clean need to get elected? Will the Minister give a full accounting of public funds used in Alma, what has been spent to date to promote that candidate, and will he file with the House a complete accounting of all the money spent to keep those five offices open?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course the Liberal Party is desperate because it has not even found a candidate yet to run in that district. When it does, we hope it does not have any difficulty finding an office, because they were experts at finding offices when they were in government.
There is no office opened as yet for the Secretary of State in Jonquiere. It was announced some months ago that the Secretary of State Department will be opening a regional office there. It is not yet open.
You are paying rent.
It will be opened later in the summer.
Next week.

The office that is now open is a temporary office. Everything has been operating properly.
I might say that when phone calls come in making inquiries about anything to do with the campaign at all, they are referred to a phone number to get information if they want it. These entrapment devices of the hon. gentleman opposite have been an absolute and complete flop.

subsubtopic: RISKS CAUSED BY NUCLEAR SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment I would like to direct my question to whomever wishes to reply for the Government.
It is common knowledge that nuclear submarines pose a threat to the environment, especially in an environment as fragile as the Arctic Ocean.
May 13, 1988

Will the federal Government initiate an open and public process to evaluate the kind of dangers to which the environment might be exposed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: RISKS CAUSED BY NUCLEAR SUBMARINES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member makes a statement in the form of a question. There has been no known leak from French, British or American nuclear submarines into the environment or the waters. They have 3,000 years of experience in their operation, and we believe it is a very good and safe system if treated properly. We intend to have safeguard mechanisms along with properly trained personnel to make sure that high level of expertise continues when we have nuclear-powered submarines in our Forces.

Mr. Speaker, there is a federal environmental assessment process but it happens to exclude the military. This project could cause far more harm than many of the projects that are evaluated. Would it not be right, given the importance of this matter, the environment, and the number of lives whose survival depends on there being no nuclear radiation in the far north, to have an environmental assessment applied to the nuclear submarine project according to the same criteria?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Associate Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat of a difficult question. The nuclear powered submarines will be out in the ocean. As the Hon. Member knows, when we are trying to neutralize used uranium in the Pickering plant in Ontario, for example, they put it into a swimming pool full of water. There are very few swimming pools in this world that are larger than the Atlantic or Pacific Oceans.

speechtext:

Yesterday, Canada Post tabled its five-year plan which indicates, among other things, that the corporation's deficit will be wiped out very shortly.
In light of this fact, could the Minister explain to the House why the policy to close down rural post offices is still being pursued? Is he prepared to make a commitment today, on behalf of his Government, to put an immediate end to this
Oral Questions
policy? Could he also give the House the assurance that all post offices closed since the Conservatives came to power will be reopened and that this will be done as soon as possible?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subsubtopic: TABLING OF 5-YEAR PLAN-CLOSURE OF POST OFFICES IN RURAL REGIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman seems to think that the crass repetition of something that is untrue will somehow, some day make it true. That is just not the case. There is no program of closing rural post offices.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF 5-YEAR PLAN-CLOSURE OF POST OFFICES IN RURAL REGIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: There certainly is.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF 5-YEAR PLAN-CLOSURE OF POST OFFICES IN RURAL REGIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows the policy. If a postmaster retires or is otherwise incapacitated, a review is instituted to see whether service can be better provided in that area by using someone in the private sector and making an arrangement with the private sector to perform a postal service. In most cases there is an improved service because the facility is open longer and a better service is provided at lower cost. There is no danger that there will be closing of rural post offices. The policy is as I have explained it, and no amount of misinformation, or whatever it is that the hon. gentleman spreads-he is from a farming area-will change that.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF 5-YEAR PLAN-CLOSURE OF POST OFFICES IN RURAL REGIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I won't apologize for my rural background, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister knows full well that I revealed in the House an internal document from Canada Post which explains how to shut down rural post offices. It is not a question of whether there is a policy of shutting them down because we know that is the case.
Let me return to the issue of suburban mail delivery. Given that this deficit is soon to be eradicated, is the Government planning to stop immediately the policy of installing new supermailboxes? Why can we not have the delivery to which Canadians have been accustomed and for which they have been paying? What is wrong with getting delivery of the mail?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):

May 13, 1988
Oral Questions
We will fight you supermailbox to supermailbox.

subsubtopic: REGISTRY OF REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. As the Minister knows, the immigration staff is creating a massive new registry of nearly 50,000 refugee claimants in Canada. Since Mr. Peter Harder, the senior assistant to the special adviser to the Minister, testified before the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration on April 26 that the proposed new refugee division will not have enough members and support staff to process this backlog in addition to the new incoming claimants, will the Minister confirm that this new registry of claimants is to be used for a new administrative review or amnesty as was proposed to the Cabinet in early 1987?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
subsubtopic: REGISTRY OF REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very interested to read this article this morning myself, but if the Toronto Star cannot understand the difference between counting people and an administrative review, I do not know how to explain it, but I will try.
This registry was set up in 1986, at the same time as the last administrative review, to give the Department and Members of this House an accurate picture of what is going on in the area of claims processing, for example, how many claimants are there and at what stage are all of these claims, and what are the characteristics of particular claims. This began in 1986. I do not in any way put that together with dealing with the current backlog.
Let me say that I will not deal with the backlog, and I have said so publicly and in the Senate committee myself, that until I have the new Bills working on behalf of refugee claimants and the immigration process in Canada to make it better and faster, I will not make any decisions on the backlog.

Mr. Speaker, the project to which the Minister refers as the "old" one has been renewed and rearranged and reorganized. This is what is reported by many people other than the Toronto Star. I am asking her, if it is not intended to use an amnesty or administrative review, if it is not intended to have these people processed by the new refugee division, which is what Mr. Peter Harder told us in the committee, why is she speeding up the deportations of people who have been under the administrative review in the past so that perhaps a few hundred will be deported before all the rest are given the amnesty?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are three ways to deal with the refugee backlog. First, would be a general amnesty. Second, would be an administrative review along the lines taken before, with more or less rigid criteria. The third would be to set up some temporary facilities for dealing with the backlog, which has been discussed as well in a number of committee hearings. I will not make a decision on those, I repeat, until the Bills are up and running. That is the most important priority for this Department.
Let me say as well that we are not speeding up deportations. There is a process in place in this country with which the Hon. Member is very familiar. He knows full well that once a claimant has been through that process, which ends for many in the Federal Court, those orders are executed. He also knows that I deal with special cases before they get to that level on a case by case basis, and will continue to do so.

[ Translation]

speechtext: Tory times are terrific times.
