unemployed from getting quick access to job retraining programs that could help meet the growing demand". When will the Government make the changes necessary so that this program will do the job that is required? When will we have some action and less rhetoric, some dollars into this program?

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Berger:
That this House condemn the Government for failing to provide adequate non-tax support for Research and Development and for its counter-productive policies and administration of tax support for Research and Development, including,
(1)	tax reform measures that discourage research and development by reducing funds available for R & D, by increasing the costs of R & D and by delaying investment in R & D facilities and delaying the introduction of new products and new processes, all of which generally impair the ability of Canadian companies to compete in global markets; and
(2)	management of R & D tax programs that has led to serious disagreements between industry and Revenue Canada over the kinds of activities that qualify for the investment tax credit for Research and Development resulting in long delays in obtaining refunds needed to finance ongoing Research and Development activities.
May 13, 1988

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) on behalf of the Liberal Party criticizes the efforts of the present Government in the area of supporting and encouraging scientific research and development in Canada. As such, it represents the height of Liberal arrogance and Liberal gall. There is quite a difference in how the Liberal Party talks when sitting in opposition as compared to when it is sitting on the government side.
Lor 33 of the 39 years between 1945 and 1984, this country was governed by Liberal Government. And what was the record of the Liberal Party when it came to scientific research and development? What was the view of those most knowledgeable in this area, the scientists themselves?
While the western industrialized countries belonging to the OECD and Japan were spending in the order of 2 to 2.5 per cent of Gross National Product on scientific research and development, Canada consistently, in all of those years, spent substantially less than 2 per cent. Notwithstanding the pleas of scientists in the university community, scientists in the private sector, scientists in government laboratories, Liberal Governments in that period refused to deal with the problem. Through all of those years, Canada was consistently last or second to last when it came to dedicating resources to scientific research and development.
That is the reality. Lor the Liberal Party now to criticize the Progressive Conservative Government, notwithstanding that it is deserving of criticism, constitutes an attitude of cynicism which is amazing.
And what about this Progressive Conservative Government? When the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was the Leader of the Official Opposition, he promised that, if elected, a Progressive Conservative Government would "move rapidly to increase those expenditures and to set the goal for expenditures at 2.5 per cent of Gross National Product".
Well, Mr. Speaker, we are now some three and a half years into the mandate of this Progressive Conservative Government, and rather than seeing an increase in scientific research and development, we see that we are spending even less, with the scientific research and development budget being down to around 1.3 to 1.5 per cent of Gross National Product.
We are now spending even less on scientific research and development than was the case when the Liberal Party formed the Government.
How does the present Conservative Government propose to deal with this very serious problem? Well, it has suggested several ways. Lirst of all, it proposed the establishment of a National Advisory Board of Science and Technology, with broad representation from the scientific community, from the university sector, from business, from labour. It was a board to
Supply
be chaired by the Prime Minister, to emphasize how important a role it would play.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that board was in fact established, and has held meetings and made recommendations. It has analysed what is being done, and it is very critical of the Government's efforts in respect of scientific research and development-and I shall come back to that later in my remarks.
Yesterday we had the announcement by the Government that it proposes to establish a new super Ministry of Industry, Science and Technology, a Department which would have $1.3 billion to spend over the next five years.
What that Department will do, no one really knows. The National Consortium of Scientific and Educational Societies has called upon the Government to use $500 million of that $1.3 billion to double the base budgets of the agencies that now fund university research. Those granting councils have not had any real increases.
To show how deficient the effort has been, and continues to be, let us compare the niggardly efforts being made in Canada, rationalized on the basis of this Government's determination to reduce the deficit, with what is being done in Japan. Let me quote from statements made by Richard Samuels, Director of the Japan Science and Technology Program at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. About the future, he said:
The real economic challenge is to generate new products and services. And that depends on a country's ability to educate and encourage people with ideas and to develop expertise in science and technology.
That's where Japan comes in. In the 1988 fiscal year alone, the Japanese Government plans to spend about $17 billion on basic scientific research, unrelated to defence. Total spending on research in Japan, including work by industry and universities, will amount to more than $100 billion.
Then he goes on to talk about the need to train students who are expert in scientific research. He says:
For example, there are 13,000 Japanese students in the U. S. and of those who will earn doctorates, 80 per cent are in science and engineering.
Japan now accounts for more than 10 per cent of the world's research spending and between 1983 and 1987 Japanese industry has opened some 80 new corporate research and development centres. Japan has had a trade surplus in technology products since 1974.
Where are we in Canada? We are not in the same ball game. We are not even in the same league. The Government proposed to deal with the problem and get greater effort by essentially freezing government expenditures on R and D and by persuading the private sector to increase its efforts substantially but it has not worked. The Government also indicated that it believes we have concentrated too much of our efforts, such as they are, on basic fundamental research and claimed that what we should be doing is putting greater efforts in research that will lead quickly to products that can be used commercially. That approach has been rejected by the two Nobel prize winners Canada has had among scientists, Dr. Hertzberg and Professor Polanyi.

May 13, 1988
Supply
Let us just look at how this supposed major effort to get industry involved is working. One of the best ideas to get industry involved was to set up an organization, Pre-carn Associates of Ottawa, headed by Gordon McNabb, to which belongs 35 major corporations in Canada including Alcan Aluminum, CAE Industries, Bell Northern Research and Falconbridge Limited. Just as it is getting going, the Government is proposing to change the federal Income Tax Act which will wipe out investment tax credits for consortium members who invest in research not directly related to their businesses.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Laurier who spoke earlier that the biggest and best research effort being done by any private sector business has been done by Bell Canada and Northern Telecom. They are part of this consortium, and their efforts to co-operate with other companies will be destroyed by the Government's very bureaucratic decision. Why did the Government make that decision? I suppose because it realized too late that the scientific tax research credit system established by the former Liberal Government was a scam. Instead of the $100 million which Mr. Lalonde, then Finance Minister, thought it would cost taxpayers, it actually cost $2.5 billion, and very little of that $2.5 billion went into real research. The present Government could have cut the $2.5 billion loss in half if it had not permitted the grandfathering of very preliminary proposals which had been made.
Let me give another example. Here we have the Canadian Advance Technology Association. Its President Roy Wood-bridge said a few days ago:
-a survey of 212 companies involved in 325 claims for R & D tax credits show that fully one-third of the claims took more than a year to be paid after they were submitted, and 22 per cent took more than 18 months.
-the Government's cumbersome approval process for tax credits seems to be an overreaction to the political embarrassment it suffered from the program's predecessor, the notoriously sloppy Scientific Research Tax Credit, or SRTC, program.
That raises another question. What we have seen in the United States, both on the East Coast and on the West Coast in California, is a host of new small companies getting started, taking some of the new basic research findings discovered at universities like Harvard, MIT, and the California Institute of Technology at Berkeley, using those ideas to develop new products which will have large sales in the increasingly technological world. These new companies are just getting started. They have as yet made no profits. If they have made no profits, tax credits are of no use to them and the Government has not dealt with that situation at all.
Let me go on, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister made a great deal about the establishment of that National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, to which I referred earlier, with broad representations. It has been in operation for some months now. It has had an opportunity to look at government programs. What did the board say? It said that without a massive increase in spending on science and technology and industry, Canada's economic future is bleak. It said that any boost in spending must be accompanied by a major effort to upgrade workers' education and skills.
What is actually happening? In fact, as the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand)
pointed out there have been cut-backs in these programs by this Government in its determination to control and reduce the deficit. There have been cut-backs in funding for training. There have been no increases in the ability of universities to train people in the scientific areas in which training is badly needed.
Let me talk for a few moments about what this advisory council on science and technology has said to the Government. It has warned that Canada's weakened industrial position will deteriorate further without a massive increase in spending on science and technology to improve competitiveness. Among the problems cited by the study are that Canada ranks lowest of seven countries in research and development spending as a proportion of Gross National Product; in scientists and engineers as part of the labour force-I gave some indication of what Japan is doing-in international patents per 1,000 people; in industries in the high-tech field with a trade surplus, and in industry funded research and development as a share of economic output. The study points out that high levels of foreign ownership in Canada contribute to this situation and that Canadian-owned firms spent 60 per cent more on research and development as a percentage of sales than foreign-owned firms.
Some years ago in discussing this same subject, I pointed out that one of the largest and most successful companies in Canada with a very large labour force, Ford Motor Company, had not one person with a Ph.D. employed in Canada doing research. I doubt that anything has changed in that respect even now. The council recommends a number of initiatives which could come into conflict with the terms of the free trade agreement, including the use of government procurement to support emerging Canadian industry, although government procurement in the United States is a major way of fostering industry and research and development.
The council also recommended targeting government funds to firms which create new technology for world markets. That proposal could be challenged as being contrary to the terms of the free trade agreement. It recommended accelerating the purchase of Canadian developed high-tech products for use in Canadian industry through low-cost financing. Those are policies we have followed in the past through our regional development programs, and they could be challenged.
The report also calls for much more emphasis on developing science and technology training as part of the business school curriculum, improvements in labour adjustment programs and the establishment of paid educational leave to assist Canadian workers to adapt to the changing needs of a high-technology economy. These suggestions came from an advisory committee, broadly based, established by this Government. Is the Government listening to those recommendations? Is the Government trying to answer those criticisms? It is not, not as far as anyone can see.
May 13, 1988

The Government plans to spend, it says, an additional $1.3 billion on science and technology over the next five years. I have not been able to find out, nor has anyone else as far as I can tell, whether in fact this extra $1.3 billion will be added to the money which was devoted to scientific research and development efforts in the past or whether it is just a recycling of old money.
We know, for example, that when the Government made its decision to get involved in a major way in space research and in the development of the space platform at a cost of $750 million, a substantial part of that $750 million was to come from cuts in scientific and research programs which had been funded in other areas in the past. We know now, as some of us warned at the time, that the $750 million would not be the actual amount needed. In fact, we knew then and were told then, both in Canada and in the United States, that the estimates for the cost of building the space platform were escalating very rapidly. Now we are told that instead of $750 million, we will have to spend $1,250 million.
Where will that increased funding come from? Will it come from further cuts to programs which are already underfunded? I ask again, as I have in the past, where there is any scientific evidence that in fact the research efforts in space will be more productive, will produce more jobs and more scientific information which can be used by Canadians, than the research done in the areas in which hundreds of thousands of Canadians have worked since Canada became a nation. We have funded scientific research in agriculture, forestry, fisheries, human resources and medicine and all that research is now being restricted in order to help fund scientific research in space. We say that that is wrong.
Let me conclude by pointing out to the Minister the concerns of the universities. University research funding, which has been inadequate in the past, and was so admitted by the Conservatives when they were in Opposition, will be further eroded and harmed by the direction this Government has taken. The universities have called for a doubling of support for scientific research and development in universities over what the Government has proposed at this time.
We support this motion, although we have no confidence that the Liberals would have done better, nor did they do any better, than the Conservatives have done in their disastrous program.

Mr. Speaker, I want to know if the Hon. Member is aware of a report prepared by a working group of officials of the Inland Revenue and Treasury of Great Britain in March of 1987. It said that for large manufacturing firms, the corporate tax system as a whole in OECD countries provides a strong incentive in Australia and Canada for firms to invest in R and D, and it goes on to talk about lesser incentives in other countries. It also says that in several countries, notably Canada and Germany, the fiscal system, broadly interpreted to include general grant programs, is much
Supply
more favourable to R and D investment by small firms than by large ones.
This report was based on OECD research and was done for the British Government. It gives us some sense of the regard with which the Canadian tax and grant systems for R and D is held by other OECD countries. I wonder if the Hon. Member was aware of that.
I listened carefully when the Hon. Member made a point about small corporations. 1 agree that we have to take a special look at that, not simply looking after the large corporations. I do not know if he heard what I tried to make clear before Question Period which was that the enhanced 35 per cent tax credit available in respect of the first $2 million of R and D expenditures of a current nature was made fully refundable in tax reform. In effect, this provides direct payments of up to $700,000 per year for eligible corporations. Making it fully refundable is the way we avoid the criticism he worried about which is that ITCs would not be useful.
Finally, the Hon. Member asked me a question in the House yesterday on another subject. He asked why so many corporations are not paying tax in Canada today, and I think today the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) asked why so many individuals are not paying tax. Then, in the last half hour, the Hon. Member made a speech about increasing tax preferences still further, increasing the flow-out provisions to allow individual investors to shelter income against tax. He seems to be talking out of both sides of his mouth.
The Hon. Member wants us to make sure that no wealthy investor escapes paying tax, but then his prescription for the R and D sector is to have more flow-out provisions which allow investors to shelter their income from further taxes. One cannot have it both ways. I would like to hear his answer on that as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister asked so many questions that I think I will have difficulty answering them all. First, there is almost universal consensus in the university and scientific community in Great Britain that the British universities and research facilities which, for almost 100 years, were at the leading edge of scientific research and were comparable to almost every other country, are now in a state of disaster. British universities are becoming second and third-grade universities because of the Thatcher Government's determination to leave everything to the private sector.
Second, as far as scientific research in Canada is concerned, we have no objection to grants or tax credits if they are really used for scientific research. However, I remind the Minister that that scam which Mr. Lalonde fathered was only the last of many attempts by Liberal Governments to encourage the private sector to do research. There is very little evidence that the Conservative Government's attempts and proposals have had any better effect.

May 13, 1988

The SRTC is gone, but we have nothing in its place. Let me put on the record some suggestions which make very good sense to me. They are contained in an article which appeared in The Toronto Star on February 9, 1988. It was written by Dr. John Evans, President and Chief Executive Officer of Allelix Incorporated. Prior to that he was President of the University of Toronto. He said, referring to corporations:
Only 2 per cent invest in R and D and of these, fewer than 7 per cent account for nearly two-thirds of all R and D performed.
But 98 per cent of Canadian companies have little appreciation of the potential of technology in improving the competitiveness of their products.
He also said:
First, industries not engaged in science and technology should be encouraged to develop technological awareness and competence through exchange programs from universities and governmental labs.
Second, industries with R and D activity should be encouraged to invest some of their R and D budget externally in university and government research groups-
He made some very concrete suggestions:
-one approach to draw in more of the 98 per cent would be an R and D levy of about 1-2 per cent of pre-tax profits on all corporations-
He then went on:
Those corporations performing R and D above this level would have their contributions refunded. The remainder would contribute unwittingly to the national support of R and D.
We are not opposed in any way to real efforts by the private sector, but we say they have to be made in conjunction with government laboratories. I remind the Minister that it was a government laboratory which developed rape seed, now a multimillion dollar product for Canadian farmers. We need support for our universities, and they are not getting it. We need support for basic research, yet the Government seems to feel that it is not necessary or should be done elsewhere.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am totally astounded that a member of the NDP can stand up and say that they want to put in place tax credits which will allow individuals and corporations to avoid paying taxes while their Leader is running around saying it is not proper for profitable companies not to pay taxes. Obviously if we go along with the suggestion made by the Hon. Member, profitable companies can use R and D tax credits to avoid paying taxes. His Leader is running around in the meanwhile saying all profitable companies should pay tax. I think he is speaking with a forked-tongue.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course all profitable corporations and all wealthy individuals, indeed all Canadians, should pay a fair share of taxes. Of course we are opposed to corporations making hundreds of millions of dollars and paying no taxes because the tax they should have paid is deferred
because they invest in new buildings or equipment and so on. Some of them may very well never pay taxes and are proud of that fact.
We are saying we can accept the idea that companies or individuals will get tax credits if they actually do scientific research and development which is useful and will increase the ability of Canada to manage in the increasingly technical world in which we are and will be living for many years to come. We are saying we support that.
What we are opposed to is the kinds of things done by past Liberal Governments, and now by a Conservative Government, which permit companies and individuals to avoid taxes by claiming they were doing scientific research when in fact they were not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to compliment my colleague, the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger), for putting forward this motion today. It is needed in order to bring out some of the inequities, indeed some of the misleading information, coming from the mouths of government Members.
In my speech today I want to zero in on the fact that the Government is reducing funds available for R and D. That certainly is true with regard to Crown corporations. At the same time, the Government is trying to give the impression that it is promoting private enterprise instead. I want to point out where that is not necessarily true either.
The Government has a habit of making high profile announcements so that people do not realize they are getting cheated. The Government makes its announcements in the midst of all kinds of publicity, with two or three cabinet Ministers in attendance or even the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Government leads Canadians to believe that it is performing wonders, but they have come to understand the Government and the way it operates. That is why it cannot maintain credibility across the country. While it pretends to be doing more for the country, it is in fact doing less in many areas.
For example, the Government says that it is promoting private enterprise and will downgrade Crown corporations. It is creating the impression that it is against public institutions because private enterprise should lead the way. Today 1 want to point out how private enterprise is still living off the Government quite substantially in some areas.
On the other hand, we have seen the Government drastically cut the budget of one of the best research institutions in this country. In the 1985 Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Government cut 50 per cent from its grants to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited in the research and development field.
Since then, it has lifted $60 million of that $100 million from Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, as well as $70 million
Supply
from the reserves of that Crown corporation. This represents a total reduction of $130 million to date. That is the Government's contribution to one of the great research and development Crown corporations of this country. At the same time it was going to reduce the contribution to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited by another $25 million this year and another $15 million next year, which would give the Government its pound of flesh of a $100 million reduction.
However, the people who manage AECL have informed the Government that it just cannot continue to operate if it loses another $25 million this year. The Government has spent months thinking about this situation and finally decided on one amendment. It will require the Crown corporation to reduce its budget by $11 million this fiscal year, but has said absolutely nothing about next year or the year after. The Crown corporation does not know what its financial future will be. What will happen to the other $29 million that the Government still wants to reduce from the budget of AECL?
Many people only think about nuclear energy when we talk about Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Not only does it deal with the peaceful use of nuclear energy, AECL does research in many fields. For example, it is at the labs of AECL in Chalk River where the new O-ring for the space shuttle has been developed. People will recall that the failure of the O-ring in the Challenger was cited as the cause of that explosion. The development of the new O-ring was done at Chalk River where AECL labs were contracted by the United States. That is just one example of the major projects it has done for international governments.
AECL also performs research and development for private enterprise. It can do this much cheaper because it already has the facilities to carry out R and D. The Government is of the opinion that if it dumps more money into major private companies, the money is better spent. The fact is that it could be duplicating research activities. Furthermore, a private enterprise company that receives substantial funds in the form of tax breaks for other incentives will likely request the right of property to that new research. Therefore, it will not be shared on a broader base in Canada.
When research and development in Canada is done in Crown corporations or government Departments, that research and development is available to all individuals and companies across the country. If they cannot perform the research and development, it can be contracted to a Crown corporation like the National Research Council. That is another Crown corporation which has suffered budget cut-backs by the Government since it took office in 1984.
Let me explain how the Government wants private enterprise to proceed and stand on its own feet. It is very interesting to analyse a financial report delivered by Andre Plourde of the Department of Economics of the University of Ottawa in October, 1987. It was prepared for Energy Options, a conference highlighted by the attendance of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse).

May 13, 1988
Supply
This financial report deals with exploration expenditure, tax expenditures and grants, northern and offshore eastern Canada. In 1985, these companies spent a total of $2,078 billion. Mr. Plourde points out that of the $2,078 billion, $1,587 billion was paid by the Government of Canada and the company paid $491 million. That is the Government's idea of private enterprise standing on its own feet without support as the Government would support Crown corporations. This means that 23.6 per cent of the total expenditures on exploration by oil and gas companies in Canada was paid for by private enterprise companies. The Government, which says that private enterprise must stand on its own feet, paid 76.4 per cent. So they are paid over 75 per cent of the money that those oil and gas exploration companies paid out during a one year term of this Government.
[DOT] (BOO)
The Government says that private enterprise must stand on its own feet, that we are going to bring Crown corporations into line. But it cuts the budget of one of the best Crown corporations in Canada, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, by 50 per cent, at the same time that it is giving 76 per cent of taxpayers' money for exploration by the oil and gas companies. Canadian citizens are certainly not seeing those benefits showing up at the gas pumps of this country.
AECL cannot write off taxes because it is not a profit organization. That is why it is a Crown corporation. But it can do the research cheaper, and the work it does for the companies is returned to those companies which in turn pay taxes to the Government. Long-term benefits is what we have to look at and the Government is looking at short-term, opportunistic politics and, of course, highlighting everything it does is its policy of leading people to think that it is doing more when in fact it is doing less.
The cost to the taxpayers of the oil and gas companies under this Government runs into the billions of dollars. Yet, it will cut the budgets of the National Research Council of Canada, which serves all people, all businesses and all corporations in Canada. It is the same with our other Crown corporations such as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. We have also seen the cancellation and closing down of the Algonquin Radio Observatory in Algonquin Park in eastern Ontario. This was done without a whimper from the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dick) who tells us he is the Minister to protect eastern Ontario. Some protection. He never uttered a word.
This Government is paying out these billions of dollars to companies which are doing research and exploration for nonrenewable resources, whereas in the nuclear energy field Canada has the safest and best record in the world for research. We have enough energy in that field alone to last for hundreds and hundreds of years. It is also cheaper.
I would like to read from an article in which Mr. de Grandpre was interviewed by a certain reporter. When asked
whether Canadian politicians help or hinder companies like Northern Telecom to compete internationally it indicated: "He snaps forward and starts speaking with animated intensity, particularly with this Government. The politicians are all saying the same thing, that we have to have more research and development capacity in Canada, as the future of this country rests on high technology products. Yet Ottawa's new tax reform package would reduce the tax rates for research and development." There it is from one of our major industrialists. He says that that amply demonstrates that politicians "don't understand how the game is played".
He is quite willing to tell you what he is doing about it. He has written letters to key politicians and is making his arguments face to face with cabinet Ministers in the present Government. As a leading member of the powerful Business Council on National Issues, he has urged other chief executives of big corporations to do likewise.
I will relate back to something I have already said, and repeat that billions of dollars are being paid out to the gas and oil companies of this country by the Government which says it wants private enterprise to stand on its own feet. Do you, Mr. Speaker, think that the large corporations that represent oil and gas will speak out against the Government as long as they are getting these kinds of tax breaks from the taxpayers of this country? They are going to leave well enough alone. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) has raised the issue of research and development for debate today. It seems to me that these issues are not debated often enough in this Chamber.
The Hon. Member and I served together on the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology. In fact, we are both founding members of that committee. The fact that that committee was only founded in this Parliament is in itself an indictment of the policies of past Liberal Governments.
Supply
Prior to the present Government taking office, there had never been a committee of this House dedicated to looking at the key issues of research, science and technology.
I have the greatest respect for the Hon. Member for Laurier, and I am pleased that he has raised the issue, inasmuch as the debate provides me with an opportunity to review for the House the Government's record in the area of research and development.
Today's economic environment is one of intense international competition. In this new order, science and technology have become the driving forces in national economies, in international trade, and within our workplaces and our homes. Over the next 25 to 30 years, these developments will produce social and economic changes as profound as those we have experienced over the last 200 years.
Innovation will clearly be the key to success, and it is industry that must lead the innovation process. But, in order to effectively execute science and technology, industry needs the support of Government. Government must provide the leadership, the co-ordination, the policies which foster a spirit of innovation.
Over the last four years, the Canadian Government has made it an urgent priority to pursue our national economic and social goals through the more effective use of science and technology. More important, it has approached that task in a thoughtful and co-ordinated fashion.
We all, of course, know that not everything can be accomplished overnight. Similarly, as our predecessors in Government showed us, little is gained by adopting a "quick fix, let's throw money at the problem" approach. The issues we must deal with are so pervasive and so fundamental that we literally require a complete rethinking and transformation of government policy, with science and technology at the centre of the government agenda.
I should like to touch briefly on some of the specific policy initiatives which the Canadian Government has brought forward, actions which underline its commitment to making technology and research and development national priorities. One of the federal Government's first tasks was to develop a national agenda for science and technology.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle), and his colleagues, held major consultations with hundreds of individuals, groups, associations, and businesses across the country, as well as with other levels of Government. Up to the time that this Government took office, there had never been a meeting of federal and provincial science Ministers. Here we are, almost at the end of the 20th century, and successive Liberal Governments up to this point had not thought it worth while for Ministers at all levels to meet in order to deal with these fundamental issues. It is little wonder that this country fell so far behind other Western countries.

May 13, 1988
Supply
Last spring an historic national science and technology policy was signed by the federal territorial and provincial Ministers. Once again, Mr. Speaker, for the first time in our history we had a national science and technology policy. We had never as a country had such a policy, a shocking indictment of the previous Government. Through this agreement all regions of the country will work together to use science and technology to promote economic, social and regional development. The policy emphasizes that governments at all levels will work in partnership with business, universities and labour to encourage the widespread diffusion of technology throughout Canada. Every effort will be made to strengthen applied research and industrial innovation. Canadian industry will be encouraged to develop strategic technologies geared toward the manufacturing, service and natural resource sectors. Canadian universities will be supported in their efforts to turn out the highly qualified people we need to develop and work with the new technologies.
For the first time federal, provincial and territorial governments have committed themselves to promote entrepreneurial activity, to recognize how critical research and development are to our economic, social and cultural future and to set about removing the barriers to research, development and innovation in Canada. The national policy was the first instalment of the science and technology framework for action. The second was launched on March 24, 1987. Innovaction is a five-track strategy which focuses Canada's science and technology efforts in five critical areas; development of strategic technologies; industrial innovation and technology diffusion; effective management of federal science and technology resources; human resources for science and technology and, perhaps most important, public awareness in science and technology.
Under Innovaction, specific initiatives have been announced to strengthen key areas of science and technology where Canada's performance has historically been weak, and to build on areas of traditional Canadian strength. These initiatives have included a $97 million federal micro-electronics strategy, a technology diffusion policy and increased funding for a number of industry support programs which have been proven effective. Our Government has also taken concrete action to ensure that Canada remains on the leading edge of space technology. Just last month the Government announced that Canada would be participating in this space station project. Our participation in this project, the most significant international space project of this century and the largest international technology development project ever undertaken, is a measure of our technological maturity as a nation. The benefits that this initiative holds for all regions of Canada for our industries and universities are immense. We estimate that more than $5 billion in space and terrestrial spin-offs and 80,000 person years of employment will be realized in Canada over the next 15 years from the space station project. I daresay that even Hon. Members opposite would have to admit that
this is a wise investment, an investment in excellence, an investment in our future.
May I say a word about the Canadian space agency which the Government has announced. It will be established to coordinate our activities in space. For perhaps the twelfth time my strong commitment is that the space agency be headquartered in the national capital region reflecting the truly national nature of Canada's space industry. Ottawa is not alone in having important space elements. Montreal is not alone in the excellence it has developed in the aerospace area. As I wrote in an article which appeared in Montreal's newspaper, The Gazette on March 31, 1987:
Significant space related industries exist now in Vancouver, Toronto, Cambridge, Ontario, Saskatoon, Winnipeg and the National Capital region.
As well as Montreal. My article went on:
The space program cannot be seen as the child of any region, without losing credibility with the rest of the country. Its headquarters must be located in politically or regionally neutral territory, so that the sub-contracting of some of its scientific facilities to the regions will not be subject to suspicions of regional favouritism.
Canada does not need a single, regional centre of excellence in Montreal.
Or anywhere else for that matter:
We need to make Canada a national centre of space science excellence. This means targeting all of our regional scientific resources to play a role in the development of our space program, and ensuring effective central scientific and political co-ordination of the program.
As I have said, working for and with all sectors of Canadian society, industry, universities, organized labour, researchers from the public and private sectors and young people is the cornerstone of our federal science and technology effort. It was one of the prime reasons for the National Conference on Technology and Innovation which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) hosted in Toronto this past January. I had the honour of attending that conference which brought together over 200 key decision makers from industry, universities and labour from across Canada.
Participants discussed some of the crucial challenges facing the economy as well as the ways in which we can take coordinated action to mount a truly national response to these challenges. I do not think I am being biased when I say that this event was a great success. I believe that most of the participants would agree with me when I say that the dialogue we forged in Toronto in January bodes well for the future.
As we speak, we are building on the consensus we achieved in Toronto and on the concerns and recommendations which were brought forward by the participants through a series of regional conferences. Regional conferences have already been held in Vancouver and Regina. The Atlantic regional conference is taking place today in Saint John and we will be convening conferences next week in Hamilton and two weeks from now in Montreal. These regional conferences have allowed more Canadians from all areas of the country to have input to this vital national dialogue. During January's national conference, the Prime Minister announced $1.3 billion in funding for new science and technology initiatives under the
May 13, 1988

Innovaction strategy. Our universities, I am pleased to say, will be the primary focus for these new funds. For example, we have already announced an $80 million National Scholarships Program to recognize and encourage our brightest young men and women to pursue studies in the sciences and engineering. We will also be establishing national networks of centres of excellence designed to support and enhance world class research in order to provide the scientific and technological base for our country's future long-term competitiveness.
Still on the subject of university research and training, the federal Government in the February, 1986, Budget introduced the first ever five-year financial plan for the granting councils totalling $3.4 billion over five years. This represents a $1.1 billion or a 50 per cent increase over the previous five-year period. A second announcement was made at the conference. While it did not receive the same volume of attention as the Prime Minister's announcement, it will likely have an even more pronounced impact on our future property as a nation.
The Minister for Science and Technology announced the launching of a $10 million national co-operative effort to increase public awareness about the importance of science and technology to Canada. This initiative will provide enhanced federal support for public awareness projects and activities undertaken by organizations outside of government. We will also be proceeding with a long-term national campaign involving governments, industry, educators and others to raise public awareness of science and technology.
Briefly, the Government's goal with respect to public awareness is to foster the development of a science culture in Canada. It is vitally important that we strengthen those cultural characteristics which can nourish the inquisitive mind the intellectual genius of our people.
More Canadians should be made aware of the significant accomplishments of our scientists, our engineers and our researchers. We also have to make more Canadians aware of the increasingly inexorable link between science and technology and economic growth and prosperity. Perhaps most important, we want to inform the young people and particularly young women of the opportunities offered by science and technology. We want to encourage them to study math and sciences and to make them aware of the exciting careers that they can pursue if they do so.
Having established a national policy and a federal strategy designed to improve our international competitiveness and create sustained economic growth and prosperity for Canada, the Government initiated a series of organizational measures to support and promote these developments. In February of last year, the Prime Minister chaired the first meeting of the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, the first time in Canada that such a board has been chaired by a Prime Minister. The board, whose membership includes some of Canada's most eminent scientists, educators and industry and labour leaders, is assessing national goals and policies for science and technology and their application to Canada's economy.
Supply
We have established for the first time a council of science and technology Ministers to monitor the implementation of the new national policy and to continue consultations with Canada's science, technology and entrepreneurial communities.
As the House will know, yesterday the Government tabled legislation for the creation of a new Department of Industry, Science and Technology. The elevation of science and technology to a senior Department is yet another clear signal of the Government's priorities. The new Department will have the mandate to work toward a closer integration of Canadian industry with Canadian scientific knowledge and technological skills. Success in this regard will require a concerted effort with the business and science communities. One of the new Department's principal objectives will be to mobilize and to catalyse this effort.
Industry will come to see the new Department as its advocate with respect to other government Departments and agencies, whether we are talking about taxation policy as we are today or trade, resource development and regulations governing, for example, transportation or communications. The new Department will seek to ensure the efficiency of Canadian production processes, technological and managerial skill levels, availability of risk capital, access to markets and many other key issues in this all-important area of research and development.
Another key activity of the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology will be to foster the development of strategic technologies such as biotechnology, information technology and advanced materials. When talking about integrating science and industrial development, the strategic technologies are of particular importance. To this end, the Government will continue to pursue such vehicles as joint investments with firms and consortia, targeted research in government laboratories, international prospecting efforts and increased funding for the training of highly qualified personnel.
As a Member from the National Capital region, may I say a word about our national laboratories. Many of these laboratories were established over 100 years ago, and I think of the research being done at the Central Experimental Farm about which I asked a question in the House today as an excellent example of that. These laboratories have been contributing to the growth of science and technology in Canada for many, many years in an effective way. The scientists and researchers who work there are dedicated public servants who are enhancing our lifestyle and improving our national effort in science and technology. They need to work, in my opinion, in a closer way than they have in the past with the universities, community colleges and business. This is a part of the Government's effort in this area, building on the strength of those laboratories which are funded to the tune of $4.4 billion in the last fiscal year, while ensuring that the technology and ideas developed there are adapted and applied in the real world where they can create jobs and new opportunities.

May 13, 1988
Supply
All of us here are familiar with phrases like the information economy and the second industrial revolution. They are used in many obscure ways, but what they mean is quite simple. Science and technology no longer can play a minor supporting role in our society. Science and technology have become the key driving forces for social and economic growth. The task which confronts Canada in restructuring our economy, rethinking our attitudes and refitting our industries is immense. It presents all sectors of our economy and society with formidable challenges, and I can say with great pride that our Government's response to these challenges has been exemplary. Our track record in science and technology is commendable. It bodes well for the future of this great nation.
In closing, I again thank the Hon. Member for Laurier for giving me the opportunity to highlight some of the Government's significant accomplishments in science and technology.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his contribution to this debate today, and I would say as well that I have enjoyed working with him on the Research, Science and Technology Committee. I would point out to him that while it is indeed the first time there has been a Research, Science and Technology Committee, there was another committee of the House on which I served for a number of years which dealt with these issues. Therefore, the question was not totally ignored, as some people might conclude from the Hon. Member's comments.
I would have appreciated it if the Hon. Member had spoken to the motion a bit more than he did. By way of this motion, I have tried to raise some legitimate concerns which have been raised with me by people who are involved in research and development in Canada. I would have liked to have heard the Hon. Member's comments on that.
I realize that we do not always solve these problems through debate in the House, but my intention today was to put this on the agenda to indicate to the Government that we were indeed watching and that there is a concern about this. Hopefully, we will be able to see some further progress in addressing some of the concerns relating to tax support for research and development.
The Hon. Member indicated that the imperatives for science and technology would require a rethinking and transformation of the Government's agenda. I think I know what he has in mind. Certainly those people who are intimately familiar with science and technology and the rapid pace of technological change tell us very often that we in Canada lack an R and D culture. He referred to the need for enhanced public awareness.
I would remind the Hon. Member that John Evans, the President of Allelix, a company doing research in biotechnology in Toronto, spoke to the National Conference on Technology and Innovation in January. He said that if we are talking about developing an R and D culture, why should the Department of Finance be excluded. Indeed, the kind of concerns that Dr. Evans raised are the ones I tried to raise by way of the motion before the House this afternoon.
The Hon. Member talked about the national science and technology policy. I would suggest to him that a statement of objectives alone does not make a policy. The so-called policy that has been put forward by this Government is a laudable statement of objectives, but it is very difficult, in reading that policy, to conclude how the Government intends to go about reaching those objectives. That is what is really required to have a meaningful policy against which we can measure the Government's performance and indeed, the performance of the economy. I would also say that one important objective has not been committed to, and that is any kind of a spending target for R and D. I would like to ask him to comment on that.
I would remind him that the Leader of his Party, before taking office, committed his Government to doubling spending on research and development over the life of his first mandate. We know that has not happened. It has gone down. Not only that, there is no mention whatsoever of a target and we do not even know if the Government considers it a worth-while objective to try and raise spending to any particular level by 1990, 1992 or 1997. Does the Hon. Member regard that omission in the so-called national science and technology policy as a serious deficiency? Does he regard it as important that such an objective should be stated by the Government along with some kind of guideline so that we can judge the progress we are making? Does he not feel that in order to make this statement of objectives a true policy we need such a target?
I put it to him that all of the items he mentioned are worthy of mention. Before I go too far, some of them I would take issue with. He talked about the granting councils. I ask him to try and be accurate when he talks about a 50 per cent increase over the previous budget. He knows very well that the budgets of the granting councils have in effect been frozen and that even with the Government's contribution to match those of the private sector, the budgets of those councils will barely keep pace with inflation. Yesterday afternoon people from the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada appeared before our committee and confirmed for the umpteenth time that that is the case. They talked about a decrease in purchasing power of the council's budgets since 1984 when the Government took office.
May 13, 1988

In any event, does he not consider, as a loyal Conservative if you will, that in business thinking we talk about a bottom line? There is a bottom line when it comes to R and D and that is the amount of spending as a percentage of the GNP. That is the common indicator used to compare the performance of one country versus another. If one goes by that bottom line, the Government, despite all its initiatives, has lead us in the wrong direction. We have moved backward in R and D spending since the last election. We have not increased scientific activity and spending on research and development.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his series of questions. I wrote down about eight of them and I doubt that in the few minutes I have available I will be able to deal with them all. However, I will deal with them quickly in the order in which he raised them.
He referred to a previous committee of this House which dealt with these issues. I was also a member of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates and, as the name implies, it was a grab-bag or catch-all committee which dealt with about 19 government agencies or Departments as I recall. It was a very disparate group of agencies which previous Governments felt did not justify their own committees. That meant we would meet perhaps once or twice a year to deal with key issues such as the estimates of the National Research Council and other agencies. That just was not good enough and I am delighted and proud that our Government recognized that and finally addressed the issue by creating this agency two and a half years ago.
The Hon. Member was concerned that I had not spoken to the motion. Let me say a few words about R and D from a tax point of view. I remind him and the House that prior to 1985 only scientific research was allowed for tax consideration, leaving aside the terrible boondoggle involved in the SRTC scam which robbed the national Treasury and taxpayers of billions of dollars. We are still counting the losses. That set back the whole process immeasurably, I am afraid. Leaving that aside, it was only in the 1985 Budget introduced by this Government that we added experimental development to the definition of research for tax purposes. That is a significant increase in the scope of eligible expenses for tax consideration. Our committee played a role in that.
I remind him that I and other members of the committee got together with the Deputy Minister of National Revenue and people like the Canadian Advanced Technology Association and, under parliamentary reform, we were able to get the kind of changes which have improved the tax situation for our high-tech firms. In fact, the level of R and D spending through the tax system is higher in Canada than in most other OECD countries. That level has increased significantly over the last four years. A number of international companies have looked to our tax system as one which encourages research and development. That is not to say it is perfect or that some of us would not like to see further changes.
Another area where I have fought a number of battles on behalf of firms in my riding concerns what in my view has

been a slow process in the Department of National Revenue in getting tax audits of scientific research and development spending so that these credits can be approved and put into the hands of the companies so they can do the new research they want to do. I am pleased to say as a result of pressure from myself and other Members, the Government announced on April 11 a process to expedite refunds for research and development claimants.
Let me talk about this culture, which was the next issue the Hon. Member raised. One of the really exciting things to me about free trade is it is going to force Canada to think more about research and development issues. Free trade is all about competitiveness and productivity. R and D is a key to attaining both those objectives without which we are destined to be, and would have been had we followed the thinking of the previous Government and the NDP, definitely in the ranks of Third World countries at the turn of the century. Free trade will force us to do a lot more R and D and be more focused in our management and spending in this area. That in itself will contribute, I am confident, to this science culture that we have to cultivate in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, wish to compliment the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) on introducing this motion today. It is important because the question of R and D and technological innovation goes to the heart of the well-being of our country and its future. All Members who have spoken in the debate this afternoon have emphasized the importance of research and development to the nation's future. Indeed, all Members agree on the importance of research and development.
Statistics show that investment in research and development guarantees more employment per dollar than any other form of investment. A study conducted by the Ministry of State for Science and Technology showed an employment growth rate 2.3 times higher than that of industries classified as performing no research. Those research-intensive industries showed a 66.5 per cent higher rate of real output. The study also showed that these industries had a 43 per cent increase in productivity and a 57 per cent slower rate in price increases.
As this and many other studies indicate, the greater the research and development, the greater the increase in productivity and job opportunities. As well, there is a substantially lower increase in cost of products produced than in industries that do not carry out research and development.

May 13, 1988
Supply
There is another dimension to research which has not been mentioned in this debate. I believe all Members will also agree that research and development also leads to a growth in human knowledge which, in itself, is an important goal. It is important that Canadians participate in this tremendous explosion of knowledge in the 20th century.
I recall listening to the famous futurologist, Buckminster Fuller, addressing a conference in which he stated that 90 per cent of all the important discoveries that have occurred in the history of the human race were made in his lifetime. There has been a tremendous acceleration in human discoveries and knowledge in almost every field which has made life so different than ever before.
Canadians are proud that there have been some very significant Canadian contributions to this growth of knowledge. Concern has also been expressed that we are not doing enough to ensure that Canadians continue to be involved in the growth of knowledge from which the Canadian economy and our way of life can benefit.
Let me emphasize that research does not only involve industrial benefits, but involves human benefits as well. An increase of human knowledge increases not only our philosophic understanding but our understanding of the universe. Increased knowledge will provide a better understanding of medicine so that we can alleviate sickness. An increase in knowledge and understanding allows us to manage our environment and reduce environmental risks. In short, knowledge in its fullest sense can contribute to the well-being of our way of life.
In a debate such as this we must also discuss the record of the present Government. I think it is fair to say that when the Government was elected in 1984 there was a fair amount of optimism and hope among scientists and the research community in Canada. After all, in his book Where / Stand, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) devoted much importance to increasing research and development. He pointed out that the goal of a Conservative Government would be to increase research and development in this country substantially. He wrote: "Even if Canada does reach the goal of 1.5 per cent of the Gross National Product by 1985 we will still lag behind other countries. In fact, if the U.S. effort were to stand still as of today, American R and D spending will be 14 times Canada's". He went on to propose that R and D under a Conservative Government should reach 2.5 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product.
The Prime Minister was right in his criticism of Canada's record on research and development. Compared to all other industrialized countries, Canada spent just a little more than Australia and Spain. In 1986, the last year for which figures are available, Canada spent 1.35 per cent of its Gross Domestic Product on research and development.
Let us compare that to the largest 12 OECD economies. In the United States, 2.89 per cent of its Gross Domestic Product went to research and development; Japan, 2.81 per cent; Sweden 2.79 per cent; Germany, 2.66 per cent; France, 2.38; United Kingdom, 2.33 per cent; Switzerland, 2.28 per cent; Netherlands, 2.06 per cent; Italy, 1.47 per cent; Australia, 1.14
per cent and Spain, 0.48 per cent. Canada did a little better than Australia and Spain.
The statistics show that we do not have a good track record in terms of what we spend on research and development as a percentage of our Gross Domestic Product.
This situation existed for years under the Liberal Government. Following the 1980 election I had the privilege of serving as the spokesperson for my Party on the Committee dealing with research and development and science and technology. There were many committee meetings in which we heard from the heads of granting agencies, the head of the National Research Council, from representatives of industry and universities as well as the scientific community. All were bemoaning the fact that there was insufficient funding.
They stated that Canada was losing its scientists and universities were unable to buy proper equipment or provide enough scholarships to keep graduate students at home. They stated that we were missing out on the growth of research and development and the job opportunities that it entailed.
We tried to get a permanent committee to deal with research and development. Even though we got the lip service from the Ministers, we never really did get any action. I must commend the present Government for at least establishing a permanent Standing Committee to deal with research and development. It is an important step in the right direction. However, I think government Members would have to admit that the Government's record is not quite what I think they intended or hoped it would be at the beginning of its term. I think it is true to say that we have not come close to the goal of 2.5 per cent goal of our gross domestic product going to research and development. The fact is that even though we have increased marginally since the Conservatives were elected, we are still at far less than the original goal.
One other area where I think we have really missed out, and the present Government is as bad as the previous Government, is the funding of the Social Sciences and the Humanities Research Council. Doing the research is one part of a process, doing the innovation is the second part which surely must be considered in devising a national strategy. We can do all the research we want, but unless we have a strategy that will help with the innovation of the newer technologies, we are going to miss the boat. That is why the Social Sciences and the Humanities Research Council must play an important role.
Unfortunately, funding for that granting agency has been significantly reduced under this Government. I must say that I find that extremely regrettable living in this day and age, an age of many changes, not just technological changes but economic changes, psychological changes and cultural changes. Surely the Social Sciences and the Humanities Research Council must play a pivitol role in allowing our society to adjust to the changes going on all around us. Cutbacks to the funding of that agency, I think, is a regressive step.
May 13, 1988

There is another area I would like to raise in this debate because I do not believe Hon. Members have made this point. Why is it we have so much less investment and expenditure in research and development than other countries? Why are our industries, in particular, investing less than other countries? I agee with government Members when they say it is not just up to the Government to increase the R and D expenditures. Industry must play a role. The Lamontagne committee, a number of years ago, pointed out part of the problem. The study by the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Technology in Ontario, printed in 1988, also points to the same problem. The major reason industry in Canada has such a low commitment to R and D is because most of our industry are branch plants. Branch plants do not do their research and development in Canada. They do their research and development at home, mainly in the United States. When we compare the amount of research done by Canadian-owned firms, we find that in many fields it is comparable to the research and development done by those same firms in in the United States.
Let me put on record some of the statistics the Ontario study came up with. For example, in business machines, the amount of R and D in the United States is 11.8 per cent. In Canada, it is 1.5 per cent. But Canadian controlled companies do 8 per cent while foreign controlled companies only do 1.3 per cent. In other machinery, in the United States it is 2.1 per cent, in Canada it is 0.9 per cent but Canadian-controlled companies do 1.1 per cent whereas foreign-controlled companies do 0.7 per cent.
In aircraft and parts, 11.4 per cent of the total outlays in the U.S. is devoted to R and D. In Canada it is 10.2 per cent, but Canadian controlled companies have a 19 per cent rate, whereas foreign controlled companies in Canada have only 5.2 per cent. It is the same in communications and equipment and drugs and medicine. The Canadian average is 4.7 per cent. Canadian controlled companies do 7.5 per cent, whereas foreign controlled companies do 3.5 per cent. It is the same situation with other chemicals. Canadian controlled companies do 2.6 per cent, whereas foreign controlled companies do 0.7 per cent, and the list goes on.
This table demonstrates that it is Canadian controlled and owned companies that are doing the industrial research and development in Canada, whereas the multinationals, the branch plants, do not do any at all. That is the major reason we have such a low R and D expenditure in Canada. The foreign controlled companies are not doing their fair share. It makes sense that a multinational corporation will have its research and development done in its home country rather than in countries like Canada.
To achieve our goal of 2.5 per cent of our gross domestic product going to research and development-and I think all Parties and all Hon. Members agree with that goal-is not a simple problem. Again, I agree with government Members when they state that just throwing money at it is not going to solve the problem. It is important and we are going to need
Supply
money and we are going to need a public commitment. But it also requires intelligence to ensure that the public money we will invest, whether it is through tax incentives or direct grants, is fine tuned and directed so it is not wasted, so it goes to a group of winners that can support a broader industrial strategy.
We must use intelligence and husbanding of our scarce resources, in this case, money, to ensure that we get the maximum benefits from our investment in R and D. Such a strategy requires the co-operation and the working together of the public sector, that is, Government and universities, provincial Governments as well as federal Governments, industry, and I should also add labour.
One of the models we could look at that is very successful in research and development is the Scandinavian countries. These countries involve labour. In Denmark and Sweden there are labour contracts where the unions insist that management introduce new techologies. The trade union movement is in the forefront of technology change in those two countries. The reason is that the working men and women in the Scandanavi-an countries recognize that if there is technological change, there is also a social net. If a newer technology does away with a job, they know they will not lose the mortgage. They know they will be retrained. They know they will get another job.
In such an atmosphere you find that the labour movement fully participates in technological innovation. It has many important contributions to make. It is the person on the shop floor who will know how best to use the equipment to get the most out of the new machines. Very often, as the Swedes have shown, it is not the individuals making decisions in the management office, but the individuals on the shop floor who, in most cases, get the most out of the new machines being introduced into the firm.
It is a model of co-operation. It is a model of working together. We can take our scientists who are working at the universities or in the labs of companies and put them together with the trade union movements, the workers, and the public sector and co-ordinate them. Such models also exist in Japan and in Germany. In fact, such models exist in the more successful industries in Canada.
I know the Government has tried to bring some of these pieces together. However, to be honest, the Government has to admit that it has not succeeded. It has not created a critical mass that has brought all the actors together so that we have a strategy and so that our money, our energies and efforts are also focused. If the Government had done that we could claim that Canada is in the forefront of technological discoveries, innovations and development. Instead, I am afraid we remain behind. We are followers rather than innovators. Unfortunately, the Government has not lived up to the expectations, the hopes and promises that existed in 1984.

May 13, 1988
Supply
I find this not from a partisan point of view but as a Canadian unfortunate. We missed an opportunity here. As so often happens, opportunities do not come again and again. Hopefully, at some future date we will have an opportunity to bring all the elements together so that we can have a policy that is focused and which can indeed make a major contribution to the well-being of our country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. It is a problem that the social sciences face.
I am part of the Finance Committee and was instrumental in getting it to make a recommendation, which was unanimously approved, to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to change the definition of science in order to broaden it. It was suggested that it should allow some of the work that is done by the social sciences and the humanities people to be included, therefore to become eligible for some types of tax credits and similar treatment. The Department of Finance is a little unwilling to do that, and in some ways understandably so.
By opening up the definition, we open up the possibilities of abuse.
For example, is motivational research which results in a different type of packaging proper research? In terms of the social sciences, motivational research is a legitimate form of research. Can what a firm spends on advertising be stuck in and be claimed to be part of legitimate research? It is a problem that I understand people in the Department of Finance have. Part of the difficulty I have in dealing with scientific research under a tax regime is that we come up against these definitions, thus opening the door to abuse.
Hon. Members have mentioned the Lalonde boondoggle which was supposed to have cost around $100 million and which ended up costing $2.5 billion. While Conservative Members point this out, I hasten also to point out that one-third of the $2.5 billion lost in tax revenues occurred when the Conservatives took office. They recognized that it was a scam. In October they tried to put a halt to it but they grandfathered it instead. This meant that if two people had an agreement written on the back of an envelope then it was still a valid agreement. The Government allowed whatever deals were made to continue until finally in May, 1985, it became too much and it shut the program down.
The whole effort by Mr. Lalonde illustrates how easy it is to abuse the tax system. Programs really have to be very well defined. Because of that the social sciences and the humanities have suffered.
The initiative of the Government to act through the income tax system as a way of boosting R and D expenditures is not the appropriate way for the social sciences to receive increased funding for the Social Sciences and Humanities Council. They must go much more into a direct granting system. Unfortunately, the government policy, both with respect to the Centres of Excellence Program and by using the income tax system, as a means of getting more R and D investment will invariably hurt the humanities and the social sciences.

But I say to him that with some of the provisions of the free trade agreement, we as Canadians will be less able to encourage government purchases and many other purchases from the private sector giving preferential treatment to Canadian companies and we will thereby decrease opportunities and decrease encouragement to those same companies to invest in R & D. We got nothing reciprocal in that area. I say to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton that he should know of several restrictive measures in the United States in defence procurement and so on which deliberately encourage United States research. There is no parallel here. Whatever little bit we had we gave away in the Prime Minister's trade deal. That is the sad reality.
May 13, 1988

The Government is saying it is doing all kinds of nice things. It produces nice brochures. I have to compliment the printer. There is always a nice picture of a Minister in them. There is one here of the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle). It is a beautiful pamphlet. I do not know what it is supposed to do. It is glossy in any case. Maybe it encourages research and development in the printing industry for the people who produce the reports. I have another pamphlet here called National Science and Technology policy. There is not much policy in it but it has lots of printing. It is a little science and technology kind of document. You could actually make a placemat out of it, it is so neat. But it does not contain anything. It is a sort of charter of economic sell-out, I guess. I really do not know what it is but it does not do anything that would encourage research and development in Canada.
I want to talk about the flow-through shares provisions that were altered in the last Budget and, of course, in the tax reform proposal as well. There is a company in my constituency which installs low head hydro generating stations. These are installed in northern Ontario and elsewhere. It is a good industry, a new one, which developed with these tax incentives. It has mini-hydro generating stations which are plugged into the grid in my Province of Ontario. They delay construction of such megaprojects as nuclear stations and so on. They provide good jobs. These stations are generally 50 megawatts or less. They are small hydraulic plants. Things have been going fairly well. A company in Toronto did the research, manufacturing and development of these mini stations and this company in my constituency had been installing them. Both of them are seriously threatened. As a matter of fact both companies may actually go down the tube. Here was a Canadian industry with research done in Canada, development done here and so on. Now it is all gone or it will be if the Minister does not do anything. I wrote to the Minister of Finance. He wrote a two page letter to me dated April 22, 1988 in which he described all the different deductions and so on. He never said he would change anything or assist this industry which had been thriving until the Government stepped in and made a mess of it.
In concluding, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) for deciding to remind Canadians of the fact that this Government has unfortunately failed to remember or deliberately chosen to forget its promises to the Canadian people. However, Mr. Speaker, there is still time. I hope the Government will take today's message to heart and take immediate action to increase research and development in this country.
