speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the good fortune to write Mr. de Grandpre's speeches when he was executive vicepresident for Bell Canada's Eastern Region and I must tell you that the language he used then was very different from the expression that the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria) seems to have given us today. I do not know why Mr. de Grandpre is frustrated, but I must tell him that when I wrote his speeches, what frustrated him most was the wastefulness of the Liberal Government of the time and also the very little research and development that were done precisely because of the total anarchy in Canada's development and science and technology policies. That is a personal comment.
I would also like to quote a document. It is a thesis prepared by ...

-the Department of Communications of the Simon Fraser University, who said exactly the same thing that Mr. de Grandpre said in 1971 and in 1972 when I was working for him and writing his speeches. The paper is entitled Policy anarchy, Industry, technology and the political agenda in Canada; the case of government support for R & D.
Mr. Leiss makes it very, very clear that this anarchy has existed since 1947 and it came to an ugly apex in 1983 under the SRTC. In his document, he quotes the Auditor General talking about R and D expenditures being out of control, but he also adds that outstanding disagreements about the meaning of the basic components of R & D activities as well as the habitual avoidance by many participants in the ongoing debate of any mention of evaluation criteria are in part the logical outcome of two decades of R & D policy anarchy.
He makes it very clear that this is a problem that existed for a long time. He also makes it very clear that something had to be done, and in that piece, he congratulates Revenue Canada for the way it has handled this absolute necessity of finding some clear evaluation criteria for these programs.
He says it is such a pity that so much money was wasted when it was required for our development, and he says also that the frequent changes in tax incentives make the task of evaluation almost impossible to perform, since various provisions are not in place long enough for meaningful comparison with R and D performance to occur. He says that this is even supposing that adequate data is being collected or analysed, and this is why, in his article, he congratulates Revenue Canada for coming up with a structure that allows for such a good analysis. He refers, for instance, to the fact that for the first time in Canadian history, there is consultation with scientists in a structured way, analysing the tax incentives which are given in these programs.

May 13, 1988

Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to point out to my hon. colleague that when he talks about election promises, one of them was to clean up government finances, and I believe that we have done so. Indeed, the policy of grants and assistance for research and development was changed precisely to fulfil this election promise of making our programs more effective and of restoring our public finances to health. For example, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced changes in May 1985, he talked about encouraging investment through tax credits that would be particularly beneficial for private companies controlled by Canadians.
So rather than burying his head in the sand and shouting that the nasty Americans are coming to take everything, he should remember one thing: we cleaned up the finances and solved the problems we had in that regard. We are now solving the problems of program effectiveness; besides, I have just come back today from a press conference held by a multinational in my riding that has invested $130 million over five years. Two hundred employees work for Erco in Buckingham, so it represents an investment of $65,000 per employee. 1 do not see why he is trying to pass his crazy ideas on to us this afternoon. It is always the same story. It is a tale of fear and exaggeration and it will do nothing to help Canada's development. Quite the contrary! Properly applied policies, such as those to clean up the public finances and those for research and development that are not based on wishful thinking, percentages tossed around at random-we really have to know whether we get results. And considering that a billion dollars has already been invested thanks to the existing R & D policy, I think that. ..

The proof is in the pudding.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no, the proof is not in the pudding, or at least not in the pudding that the Hon. Member is trying to make us eat here today. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, as my colleague from Laurier so eloquently says.
I was talking about the comments of Mr. de Grandpre on the Minister's recent tax reform. That did not exist 20 years ago, though the Hon. Member can try to make us believe that.
Let me read some of those comments again. I kind of like reading them. The article reads:
Yet Ottawa's new tax reform package would reduce the tax breaks for R &
D. That, he says, amply demonstrates that politicians "don't understand how
the game is played."
When someone asks Mr. de Grandpre if he could have a job, he will say: "Sorry, but we're not expanding our R and D
facilities in Canada". He'll ask why, and the answer is: "Well, because the Government, this Government, has introduced this stupid piece of legislation". That refers to this present Government's tax reform package, not the package of 1969, 1972 or 1947. It is not the package of 1931 or any of those other years before I was born. This is something that is going on right now. This is the April 1988 edition of the Report on Business magazine, an interview with Mr. Jean de Grandpre.
The Hon. Member says that we are fear-mongering. She thinks that my comments are a tad partisan. That is okay, as unrealistic as that proposition may be. However, surely she cannot say the same thing about the Conference Board of Canada which has prepared a serious document on Research and Development entitled Research and Development Impacts of Corporate Income Tax Reform, and it dealt with all these cancellations in construction facilities, one of them which is right in Calgary. I see that an Hon. Member from Calgary is over there.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 know that it is hard to take. If I were a Tory, perhaps I would have a hard time taking it too. However, I have the good fortune of not being a Tory, thank God for that.
